Description: Don Cheadle was James Rhodes, AKA War Machine, a character in the Marvel Universe and is paralysed in an encounter with Vision so relies on leg braces created by Tony Stark to enable him to stand and walk. Appearing in The Falcon and the Winter Soldier, Avengers: Endgame, Avengers: Infinity War, Captain America: Civil War and Avengers: Age of Ultron. Rhodes acquires a motor disability in Captain America: Civil War after a mid-air accident leaves him with spinal trauma. He uses mechanical leg braces to walk and maintain mobility. His condition is permanent and visibly affects his movement in subsequent films. Rhodes remains an active Avenger and military liaison post-injury. His disability is acknowledged but not deeply explored. He continues to operate the War Machine suit and participate in combat, with his impairment largely mitigated by technology. His injury is used to heighten stakes and underscore the risks of superhero conflict, but not as a lens for lived experience, which is a missed opportunity to add depth to an otherwise two dimensional character. Don Cheadle is not physically disabled, making this a clear case of cripping-up. The portrayal leans heavily on assistive tech as a narrative fix, sidelining authentic exploration of disability. Rhodes’ character lacks depth in terms of personal adaptation, emotional impact, prejudice, self-confidence or social barriers.
Name: Don Cheadle

Description: Sebastian Stan played Bucky Barnes AKA the Winter Soldier, a character from the Marvel Universe who is an amputee. Appeared in The Falcon and the Winter Soldier, Avengers: Endgame, Avengers: Infinity War, Black Panther, Captain America: Civil War, Ant-Man, Captain America: The Winter Soldier, Captain America: The First Avenger and Captain America: Super Soldier. Bucky loses his left arm during WWII and receives a cybernetic replacement from Hydra. His prosthetic is central to his identity as the Winter Soldier. The arm is upgraded multiple times and functions as both weapon and symbol of his trauma. Bucky’s disability is entwined with his transformation into a brainwashed assassin. His prosthetic arm is a visual marker of his altered state and is often used to signify violence, control, and dehumanisation. In The Falcon and the Winter Soldier, his rehabilitation arc includes therapy and attempts to reclaim agency, but the arm remains a tool of combat rather than a lived experience. Sebastian Stan is non-disabled, and the portrayal of limb difference is stylised and instrumentalized. The arm is treated as a superpower, not a disability fixed by an overcompensating assistive technology, and lacks any authentic depiction of prosthetic use, adaptation, or social stigma. The narrative avoids exploring disability identity, instead using the prosthetic as a metaphor for unhinged power and control.
Name: Sebastian Stan

Description: Hugh Grant played an Oompa Loompa in Wonka (2023), sparked outrage from the community of people of short stature. Oompa Loompas have historically been portrayed by actors with dwarfism, with their short stature being a defining visual and cultural trait. Lofty is introduced as a whimsical, mysterious character who helps Wonka navigate the chocolate world. His stature is used for comic effect and visual novelty, continuing the tradition of Oompa Loompas as fantastical beings. However, the character’s physicality is central to his identity and screen presence. The casting sparked backlash from actors with dwarfism, including George Coppen, who stated: “We feel like we are being pushed out of the industry we love.” Critics argued that the role could and should have gone to a performer with lived experience of dwarfism. The use of CGI to simulate short stature is seen as a form of digital cripping-up, reinforcing exclusion and undermining opportunities for disabled actors in fantasy and mainstream roles.
Name: Hugh Grant

Description: Charlie Rowe played  Nate Gibson from the film Gigi & Nate (2022) about a young man with serious mobility issues. Nate Gibson becomes quadriplegic after a viral infection, resulting in profound mobility impairment. He uses a wheelchair and requires assistance with daily tasks. The film centers on his adjustment to life with a disability and his bond with a service monkey. Nate is the emotional core of the film. His disability is portrayed as a life-altering event that reshapes his relationships, identity, and aspirations. The narrative leans heavily on inspiration, with the service animal framed as a symbol of hope and recovery. Charlie Rowe is not disabled, making this a clear case of cripping-up. The film has been criticized for its reliance on able-bodied performance and its sentimental framing of disability. While it aims to raise awareness, it does so through a lens of pity and triumph, rather than authentic lived experience. The absence of a disabled lead actor undermined the film’s credibility.
Name: Charlie Rowe

Description: Jack Dylan Grazer played Freddy Freeman in Shazam! (2019) and Shazam! Fury of the Gods (2023), a character from the DC Universe has profound mobility issues in the comics. Freddy Freeman has a physical disability that affects his mobility. He uses a crutch and walks with difficulty. In DC Comics, Freddy’s condition is more pronounced, and he is often depicted as having profound mobility limitations. Freddy is portrayed as witty, loyal, and emotionally resilient. His disability is acknowledged but not deeply explored. When he transforms into his superhero alter ego (Captain Marvel Jr.), he becomes physically able-bodied, reinforcing a perceived duality between weakness and power. Jack Dylan Grazer is non-disabled, and the portrayal has drawn criticism for glossing over the realities of mobility impairment, where disability is “cured” through magic. The casting missed an opportunity to authentically represent disabled youth in a genre that rarely includes them, and the writing could have explored Freddie's lived experience of his two identities.
Name: Jack Dylan Grazer

Description: Benedict Cumberbatch first appeared as Doctor Stephen Strange in the Marvel Universe in Doctor Strange (2016) and then in Thor: Ragnarok (2017), Avengers: Infinity War (2018), Spider-Man: No Way Home (2021) and Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness (2022). Doctor Strange is motor impaired which is why he stopped being a surgeon in his origin story. Doctor Strange acquires a motor impairment following a car crash that causes severe nerve damage to his hands. Despite multiple surgeries, he loses fine motor control, ending his career as a neurosurgeon. The impairment is permanent and visibly affects his hand function. Strange’s disability is the catalyst for his transformation, from arrogant surgeon to mystical protector. However, once he becomes the Sorcerer Supreme, his impairment is largely sidelined. His magical abilities allow him to perform complex gestures and combat manoeuvres, effectively bypassing the limitations of his injury. The disability is rarely referenced after the origin arc. Cumberbatch is not disabled, making this a clear case of both cripping-up and erasure. Benedict Cumberbatch appeared in Richard III in The Hollow Crown (2016). In real life Richard III had scoliosis, but in Shakespeare's plays Richard's disability is accentuated and exaggerated, and his role is the first script ever to explore ableism. Historically, Richard III had scoliosis, a curvature of the spine. In Shakespeare’s play, this is exaggerated into a grotesque deformity, “rudely stamped,” “unfinished,” and “deformed”, used as a visual metaphor for moral corruption. The character is often portrayed with a limp, hunchback, or withered arm. Richard’s disability is central to his identity and villainy. He internalises society’s rejection and uses it to justify his manipulation and cruelty. Shakespeare’s text is one of the earliest dramatic explorations of ableism, explicitly linking physical difference to social exclusion and psychological trauma. Cumberbatch’s portrayal in The Hollow Crown was praised for its psychological nuance but still involved a non-disabled actor simulating disability. While the production attempted to humanize Richard and explore his trauma, it perpetuated the tradition of cripping-up. As disability scholars note, the role has historically been denied to disabled actors, despite being one of the most prominent disabled characters in the canon.
Name: Benedict Cumberbatch

Description: Nathan Darrow was cast as Victor Fries, AKA Mr Freeze in Gotham (2015 to 2018). Mr Freeze has an armoured prosthetic suit for life support and assistive technology. Without this tech he cannot do anything or survive. Mr. Freeze requires a life-support exosuit to survive due to a cryogenic accident. Without it, his body cannot function in normal temperatures. His condition is a form of extreme environmental dependency, akin to ventilator or assistive tech reliance. Fries is portrayed as a tragic villain, driven by love for his terminally ill wife. His disability isolates him physically and emotionally, reinforcing his descent into villainy. The suit becomes both a symbol of his loss and a source of power, enabling him to weaponize his condition. Nathan Darrow is non-disabled, and the role relies on stylised costuming and effects rather than authentic embodiment. The absence of a disabled actor in a role so defined by assistive technology reflects missed opportunities for authentic representation.
Name: Nathan Darrow

Description: Jeremy Renner was cast as Clint Barton AKA Hawkeye from the Marvel Universe is Deaf, which is arguably one of the most interesting aspects of the character.  In Marvel comics, Hawkeye is canonically deaf, using hearing aids and lipreading. His deafness is integral to his identity and resilience. In the MCU, this was erased for years. Only in the 2021 Hawkeye series was hearing loss reintroduced, attributed to cumulative trauma from battles. Hawkeye is a founding Avenger, often portrayed as the “everyman” among superpowered peers. His deafness in the comics adds depth, showing how a disabled hero adapts and thrives. In the MCU, this was sidelined until fan pressure and disability advocacy led to partial restoration. Casting a hearing actor in a deaf role, even after restoring the disability undermines authentic representation. The MCU missed an opportunity to cast a deaf actor or consult more deeply with the deaf community, especially given the success of Echo (Alaqua Cox) as a deaf superhero.
Name: Jeremy Renner

Description: Stephen Merchant cast as Caliban in Logan (2017). Caliban is a clever character as he is a metaphor for a lot of what is a disabled lived experience, where things like sunlight, that we all take for granted, are harmful to him. Caliban has extreme photosensitivity, making sunlight harmful and potentially fatal. This condition isolates him and limits his mobility. His disability is metaphorical, representing vulnerability, stigma, and adaptation. Caliban is a caregiver and moral compass, assisting Logan and Xavier while grappling with his own limitations. His condition shapes his worldview and choices, especially his sacrifice to protect others. Merchant is not disabled, and Caliban’s portrayal avoids pity, but still his pain and isolation are performed, not embodied. Authentic casting could have deepened the metaphor, aligning Caliban’s emotional arc with real-world disability narratives of exclusion and agency.
Name: Stephen Merchant

Description: Anne Hathaway was cast as the Grand High Witch in The Witches (2020), and the witches all had visible physical disabilities such as limb differences.  The character was designed to have limb differences, three fingers on each hand and toe-less feet, which was not present in the original Roald Dahl book or the 1990 film adaptation. The Grand High Witch is the villain, and her limb difference was used as a visual marker of evil, equating physical difference with monstrosity. Disability advocates, including Paralympians and limb difference charities, condemned the portrayal as stigmatizing. Hathaway issued a public apology, acknowledging the pain caused and pledging to “do better”.
Name: Anne Hathaway

Description: Timothy Dalton was cast as Chief in Doom Patrol (2019 to 2023). Chief is a wheelchair user, a central aspect of his character in comics and screen adaptations. He’s a scientist and leader of the Doom Patrol, often depicted as morally ambiguous. Chief’s disability is not incidental, it’s part of his identity and informs his worldview. His leadership and intellect challenge stereotypes, but the casting choice dilutes this impact. Dalton is not a wheelchair user, and no visible effort was made to cast authentically. The show’s progressive tone contrasts with this casting, revealing a gap between narrative ambition and representational practice. Disability portrayal in Doom Patrol is problematic with Robotman and Cyborg, both disabled characters, being cast with non-disabled actors.
Name: Timothy Dalton

Description: Patrick Stewart was cast as Professor X in the X-Men series, a character who is partially paralysed and is a wheelchair user. Xavier is a wheelchair user, one of the most iconic disabled characters in fiction. His disability is central to his role as mentor, strategist, and moral compass of the X-Men. Xavier’s mobility impairment symbolises resilience and intellect over brute force. His leadership of mutants, many of whom face discrimination, parallels real-world disability advocacy and the experience of the otherness and discrimination many disabled people face in their daily lives.
Name: Patrick Stewart

Description: Dakota Johnson was Cassandra Webb in Madame Web (2024), a character who is both blind and paralysed.  In comic canon, Cassandra Webb is blind and paralysed due to a severe neuromuscular condition (myasthenia gravis). She uses a life-support chair and possesses clairvoyant abilities. In the film, her origin story is altered: she is not disabled until the end of the movie, and her powers are foregrounded over her impairment. Webb’s disability is minimised in the film adaptation. Dakota Johnson plays her as an able-bodied paramedic for most of the runtime, with disability introduced only briefly and ambiguously. The character’s clairvoyance is emphasised, while her physical limitations are downplayed or deferred. This is often referred to as Disability Erasure when a well know historical, literary, screen or comic book character has their disability downplayed or removed which can have the adverse effect of making them less interesting to the audience. This can also be seen as offensive by disabled audiences and a reinforcement of ableist attitudes. This might be to too complex to accurately cast, but an actor with the experience of being a disabled person with either vision or mobility issues would be more suitable if the character is more aligned with the original text.
Name: Dakota Johnson

Description: Aaron Paul was cast as Adam Niskar in Quad (2020). Adam Niskar was a real-life quadriplegic who sustained a spinal cord injury in a diving accident. The character is depicted as having complete paralysis from the neck down, requiring full-time care and assistive technology. The film follows Adam’s journey from trauma to adaptation, emphasising emotional resilience and personal growth. It’s a biographical drama, meaning the disability is central to the story and based on lived experience. Aaron Paul is not disabled, and the role involves mimicking quadriplegia rather than embodying it. Critics noted the absence of disabled talent in a story that could have empowered authentic representation. The film’s emotional arc focused on the barriers disabled people have to overcome, but non-authentic casting approached this through a non-disabled lens, which was a missed creative opportunity.
Name: Aaron Paul

Description: Colin Farrell has been cast as The Penguin in The Batman (2022) and The Penguin (2024). The Penguin (Oswald Cobblepot) has mobility impairments, often depicted with a limp, hunched posture, and physical asymmetry. In some versions, he uses assistive devices like canes or braces. A classic villain in the Batman universe, Penguin’s disability is part of his visual identity and symbolic of his outsider status. Farrell’s portrayal emphasises grotesque transformation, prosthetics, fat suits, and heavy makeup, to achieve the look. Farrell is not disabled. Despite acclaim for the performance, the casting choice missed an opportunity for authentic embodiment, even though this is one of the rare occasions where disability was brilliantly played by a non-disabled actor.
Name: Colin Farrell

Description: Jude Law was cast as Captain Hook is an amputee in Peter Pan & Wendy (2023). Captain Hook is an amputee, traditionally depicted with a prosthetic hook replacing one hand. His disability is iconic and central to his visual identity. Hook is the antagonist in the Peter Pan universe, often portrayed as bitter, vengeful, and physically marked by his disability. Law’s version aimed to humanise Hook, exploring emotional depth and trauma. The film did not consult disability advocates or cast disabled talent, despite Hook being one of the most famous disabled characters in children’s literature. The lack of a cure at the curtain call through authentic casting could have provided a depth to the character that has yet to be seen, and gone to the emotional depths this character potentially has.
Name: Jude Law

Description: Was cast as Stick in the Daredevil series. The character is the old blind mentor of Daredevil and the actor is not vision impaired. Stick's blindness, relying on heightened senses and martial arts mastery, added depth to a character that could have been further exploited with a vision impaired actor. His blindness is also integral to his identity and philosophy. Stick’s disability is portrayed as a source of strength and wisdom, aligning with the “blind master” archetype seen in series like Kung Fu. Scott Glenn, who played Stick, is not blind. The casting reinforced the pattern of non-disabled actors portraying blind characters, despite the availability of blind or vision impaired talent.
Name: Scott Glenn

Description: Colton Dunn was cast as Garrett in Superstore (2015 to 2021). Garrett is a wheelchair user, paralyzed from the waist down. The show never specifies the cause, and his disability is treated as incidental to the plot, but it does add context and subtext to the character and several key scenes. Garrett is a sardonic, laid-back employee at Cloud 9. His disability is rarely addressed directly, and he’s portrayed as socially active, humorous, and romantically involved. The character avoids “inspiration porn” and is not defined by his disability, however the inauthentic casting takes away a lot of what this character achieved in terms of portrayal.  Colton Dunn is not disabled, and the casting drew criticism for cripping-up a role that could have gone to a wheelchair user.
Name: Colton Dunn

Description: Neil Sandlands was cast as The Thinker in the TV Series The Flash (2017 to 2018), a comic book character who has profound motor disabilities. Clifford DeVoe, aka The Thinker, has advanced ALS, resulting in profound motor disability. He uses a wheelchair and assistive tech to communicate and control his environment. The Thinker is the season’s main antagonist, a genius whose body deteriorates while his mind remains powerful. His disability is central to his arc, driving his quest for control and survival. Authentic casting could have added a postmodernist truth and depth to the character.
Name: Neil Sandilands

Description: Karen Gillan was cast as Nebula in the Marvel Universe who has many physical disabilities, so has many prosthetics and accelerated assistive technologies. The character appears in Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3 (2023), The Guardians of the Galaxy Holiday Special (2022),  Thor: Love and Thunder (2022), Avengers: Endgame (2019),  Avengers: Infinity War (2018), Guardians of the Galaxy: Vol. 2 (2017) and Guardians of the Galaxy (2014). Nebula is an amputee and prosthetic user, with extensive cybernetic enhancements. Her body has been forcibly modified, resulting in chronic pain and trauma. She embodies themes of bodily autonomy, recovery, and resilience. Initially a villain, Nebula evolves into a hero. Her disability is both literal and metaphorical—representing survival, adaptation, and emotional depth. Her arc includes reconciliation, self-worth, and agency. Gillan is not disabled, and the role relies heavily on prosthetics and visual effects. Nebula's her portrayal lacks lived experience, especially in scenes of pain and embodiment, a layer that could have added depth and context not only to the performance but to the production and publicity. Authentic casting could have deepened the character’s emotional resonance with the audience's relationship by offering a more grounded portrayal of disability and trauma.
Name: Karen Gillan

Description: Ray Fisher was cast as Cyborg in Zac Snyder's Justice League (2021).  Victor Stone is profoundly disabled after a near-fatal accident. His body is sustained by a prosthetic exosuit with life-support and weaponised tech. Without it, he cannot survive or function. Cyborg is central to the film’s emotional arc. His disability is not erased, it’s explored through grief, adaptation, and empowerment. Snyder’s version foregrounds Victor’s humanity, agency, and emotional depth. Fisher is not disabled, but his performance and advocacy reframed Cyborg as a symbol of disability pride and resilience. While not authentically cast, the narrative lens is closer to lived experience, offering a rare example of disability portrayed with dignity and complexity. Authentic casting could have brought a greater insight to this intention, giving a greater truth to the performance.
Name: Ray Fisher

Description: Lana Condor was cast as Jubilation Lee in X-Men: Apocalypse (2016). In some comic iterations, Jubilee is coded as neurodivergent, with traits associated with ADHD or learning differences, impulsivity, emotional intensity, and sensory sensitivity. These traits are not explicitly diagnosed, but resonate with neurodiverse readers and became a core aspect of her character. Lana Condor is not neurodivergent, and the film does not acknowledge Jubilee’s cognitive traits. This is a case of erasure by omission: the character’s neurodiverse coding is flattened into a generic teen sidekick.
Name: Lana Condor
Known For: To All the Boys I've Loved Before

Description: J. August Richards was cast as Deathlock in Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D. (2013 to 2018). Deathlok (Mike Peterson) is canonically a cyborg with extensive prosthetics, including a robotic arm and life-sustaining implants.His body is reconstructed after trauma, making him dependent on assistive technology. In the series, Peterson becomes Deathlok after a near-death experience. His transformation is central to his arc, struggling with autonomy, identity, and control. The show explores themes of bodily integrity and surveillance, but not through a disability lens which is what at times anchors the character. Richards is not disabled, and the prosthetics are treated as sci-fi enhancements rather than disability accommodations. The show sidesteps the disability metaphor, framing Deathlok as a weaponised asset rather than a including the duality of a disabled person navigating embodiment. This is a erasure of a character's disability identity: the tech is visible, but the lived experience of prosthetic use and identity are absent. What could have been an interesting character has little depth. Authentic casting could have grounded the character’s trauma and agency in real-world disability narratives.
Name: J. August Richards

Description: Simone Missick was cast as Misty Knight in Luke Cage (2016 to 2018) and The Defenders (2017). Misty Knight loses her arm in The Defenders and receives a bionic prosthetic from Stark Industries. She is a Black disabled woman with a visible limb difference, a rarity in superhero media. Misty’s arc includes grief, adaptation, and reclaiming power. Her prosthetic becomes a symbol of resilience and justice. She continues to work as a detective, challenging assumptions about capability. Missick is not an amputee, but her portrayal is widely praised for emphasising strength. The show consulted with disability advisors and gave Misty narrative agency, though it still centres through a non-disabled lens, which is a missed creative opportunity. Authentic casting could have deepened the audience's relationship with the character, especially in scenes of physical adjustment and emotional processing.
Name: Simone Missick

Description: Rhys Ifans was cast as Dr. Curt Connors in The Amazing Spider-Man (2012). Dr. Connors is a one-armed scientist who experiments with reptilian DNA to regenerate his limb. His disability is central to his motivation and eventual transformation into The Lizard. Connors’ desire to “fix” himself drives the plot. His disability is framed as a deficiency to be overcome, leading to monstrous consequences.The Lizard becomes a metaphor for unchecked ambition and self-loathing. Ifans is not disabled, and by casting a non-disabled actor reinforcing a narrative suggests that disability is something to be cured or escaped, rather than accepted. Authentic casting could have challenged this framing, offering a more nuanced portrayal of ambition, embodiment, and scientific ethics.
Name: Rhys Ifans

Description: Bryan Cranston was cast as Philip Lacasse in The Upside (2017). Philip Lacasse is a quadriplegic, paralysed from the neck down after a paragliding accident. He requires full-time care and uses a motorised wheelchair and assistive devices for daily living. The film is a remake of The Intouchables and centers on the friendship between Philip and his caregiver, Dell. Philip’s disability is central to the plot, but the emotional arc focuses more on Dell’s redemption than Philip’s autonomy. Cranston is not disabled, and the role involves mimicking quadriplegia, a textbook case of cripping-up. By casting a non-disabled actor as a disabled character it accentuates an idea that a disabled character is there to catalyse growth in a non-disabled protagonist. Authentic casting could have shifted the lens from performance of disability to embodiment, offering a more grounded portrayal of agency, intimacy, and interdependence.
Name: Bryan Cranston

Description: Manu Bennett was cast as Slade Wilson AKA Deathstroke in Arrow Arrow (2012–2020). Slade Wilson is vision impaired, having lost one eye in combat. He wears an eyepatch and has reduced depth perception. His impairment is both physical and symbolic, marking his transformation into a vengeful antihero. Slade begins as a mentor and ally to Oliver Queen but becomes a major antagonist. His disability is tied to his downfall associating disfigurement with moral decline. Bennett is not vision impaired, and the role uses the eyepatch as a visual shorthand for trauma and menace. Authentic casting could have challenged any view that this character has an ableist framing, offering a portrayal rooted in lived experience, at rather than symbolic othering.
Name: Manu Bennett

Description: Brendan Fraser as Cliff Steel AKA Robot Man in Doom Patrol (2019–2023) who has an armoured prosthetic suit of life support and assistive technology. Cliff is a former race car driver whose brain is transplanted into a robotic body after a catastrophic accident. He has no physical sensation and is entirely dependent on assistive technology for movement and survival. Cliff’s arc explores loss of embodiment, identity, and emotional regulation. His disability is metaphorical and literal as he struggles with anger, alienation, and reconnection with his daughter. Fraser is not disabled, and the role is split between voice acting and physical performance by a body double. While the show is praised for its emotional depth and disability metaphors, it still centers a non-disabled lens. Authentic casting could have brought nuance to Cliff’s physicality and emotional processing, especially in scenes of frustration and adaptation.
Name: Brendan Fraser

Description: Steve Bacic was cast as Sonus AKA Discord in Arrow (2017). Sonus is a deaf character in the comics, whose sonic powers emerge after being deafened by Black Canary’s attack. His deafness is central to his origin and powers, making him one of the few deaf villains in DC lore. In Arrow, Sonus is reimagined as a metahuman drug dealer with sonic abilities, but his deafness is not acknowledged. The show erases his disability entirely, reframing him as a generic antagonist. Steve Bacic is not deaf, and the character’s disability was removed from the screen adaptation. This is a clear case of disability erasure, where a canonically disabled character is rewritten as non-disabled to enable non-disabled casting. Authentic casting and retention of Sonus’s deafness could have challenged the idea of disability as weakness, reframing sonic power as adaptation rather than anomaly.
Name: Steve Bacic

Description: Alex Collins was cast as Dr. Charles McNider / Doctor Mid-Nite in Stargirl (2020–2021).  McNider is blind, using special goggles to see in darkness. He’s widely recognized as the first disabled superhero in comics (debuting in 1941). His blindness is integral to his identity and powers. In Stargirl, McNider appears as a mentor figure and AI presence, later revealed to be alive. His blindness is acknowledged but not deeply explored; the focus is on his intellect and legacy. Alex Collins is not vision impaired, and the role involves mimicking blindness. While McNider is portrayed respectfully, the casting maintains a non-disabled lens, missing the opportunity to show blind embodiment as well as both social and physical navigation. Authentic casting could have reframed McNider’s mentorship through lived experience, offering grounded representation
Name: Alex Collins

Description: Samuel L. Jackson as Nick Fury in the Marvel Universe. Fury is vision impaired, having lost his left eye. He wears an eyepatch and has facial scarring. His impairment is symbolic of his hardened persona and tactical edge. Fury is the architect of the Avengers Initiative, a master strategist and spy. His missing eye is referenced in jokes and flashbacks but rarely explored as a disability. Jackson is not vision impaired, and the role treats the eyepatch as aesthetic branding rather than disability. Authentic casting could have grounded Fury’s resilience in lived experience, reframing his impairment as part of his tactical brilliance rather than surface visual flair. Samuel L. Jackson was also cast as Elijah Price / Glass in Glass (2019). Price has Type I osteogenesis imperfecta, a rare condition causing brittle bones and frequent fractures. He is also mobility impaired, using a wheelchair throughout the film. Glass is a super-intelligent villain who believes his fragility proves the existence of superhumans. His disability is central to his philosophy and identity, driving the trilogy’s narrative arc. Jackson is not disabled, and the role involves mimicking chronic pain and mobility impairment. Authentic casting could have reframed Price’s intellect and trauma through embodied experience, challenging any notion that disability breeds malice.
Name: Samuel L. Jackson

Description: Forest Whitaker cast as Saw Gerrera in Rogue One: A Star Wars Story (2016). Gerrera is a war veteran with extensive physical injuries, including prosthetic limbs, respiratory support, and mobility impairment. His body is visibly augmented due to trauma sustained in combat. Gerrera is a radical rebel leader, estranged from the mainstream Rebellion. His physical condition reflects the toll of prolonged resistance and ideological extremism. His augmentations are symbolic of sacrifice and survival, but also alienation. Whitaker is not disabled, and the role uses prosthetics and laboured movement to signal trauma. Authentic casting could have deepened the audience's relationship with the character through a better informed embodiment of resilience and isolation.
Name: Forest Whitaker

Description: Perry Mattfield cast as Murphy in, In The Dark (2019–2022). Murphy is blind, navigating life with a guide dog and adaptive strategies. Her blindness is central to the plot and character identity. Murphy is a flawed, complex protagonist, sarcastic, reckless, and emotionally guarded. The show explores her relationships, independence, and involvement in a murder investigation. Mattfeld is not blind, and the casting sparked significant backlash from disability advocates. Authentic casting would have removed the performance barrier, allowing Murphy’s embodiment to reflect real lived experience, especially in scenes of navigation, intimacy, and emotional vulnerability.
Name: Perry Mattfeld

Description: Stephen Lang cast in Don’t Breathe (2016) where he played the role of Norman.  Norman is blind, relying on his other senses and tactical awareness to defend his home. His blindness is central to the film’s suspense and reversal of expectations. Initially portrayed as a victim, Norman becomes a violent antagonist. His blindness is used to amplify horror and unpredictability. The sequel in 2021 attempts to humanise him, but the disability remains a plot device. Lang is not blind, and the role uses blindness as aesthetic tension rather than character depth, however authentic casting  could have brought that as subtext. Authentic casting could have reframed Norman’s embodiment as complex in the way Richard III is, bringing in his past and experiences of ableism and otherness as narrative layers.
Name: Stephen Lang

Description: Craig Roberts was cast in The Fundamentals of Caring (2016). Playing a wheelchair user. Trevor is a teenager with Duchenne muscular dystrophy, a progressive condition that causes muscle degeneration and requires full-time wheelchair use and personal care. Trevor’s story centers on emotional growth, independence, and connection. His disability is not the plot’s obstacle but the context for exploring trust, humour, and agency in his relationship with his caregiver. Roberts is not disabled, and while the film avoids pity or schmaltz, the performance remains a simulation. Critics praised the emotional realism, but disabled audiences noted the absence of embodied experience.  Authentic casting could have reframed Trevor’s sarcasm and vulnerability as lived traits, deepening the bond with Paul Rudd’s character and allowing audiences to witness genuine interdependence. This would also have positioned the film as a landmark in inclusive casting, especially given its Sundance premiere and Netflix distribution. Disabled actors can play progressive conditions such as in the BBC's series Better (2022), however this is down to the capability of the individual actor and creative approach taken by the director.
Name: Craig Roberts

Description: Charlize Theron was cast as Imperator Furiosa in Mad Max: Fury Road (2015). Furiosa is a below-elbow amputee, using a mechanical prosthetic arm. Her disability is visible and integrated into her combat and survival skills. Furiosa is the film’s moral and tactical center, leading a rebellion, protecting the vulnerable, and challenging patriarchal control. Her prosthetic is not fetishized; it’s functional and symbolic of resilience. Theron is not an amputee, and while her portrayal is widely celebrated, the casting missed a chance to redefine action heroines through authentic embodiment. A disabled actor could have brought new physicality to Furiosa’s movements, reframing her relationships with Max and the Wives through recognisable authenticity. This would have elevated the film’s feminist and anti-ableist themes, offering a publicity opportunity around inclusive action cinema—especially given its Oscar success and cult status.
Name: Charlize Theron

Description: Sofia Boutella was cast as Gazelle in Kingsman: The Secret Service (2014). Gazelle is a double amputee, using blade prosthetics as weapons. Her disability is stylised part of her combat identity and visual spectacle. She’s the henchwoman to the main villain, with minimal dialogue but high-impact action scenes. Her prosthetics are central to her fighting style and aesthetic. Boutella is not an amputee, and the role treats disability as visual novelty. Authentic casting could have transformed Gazelle from a stylised threat into a complex character, with movement and presence shaped by real-world prosthetic use. This would have reframed her relationship with Valentine and the Kingsman agents—not as spectacle, but as embodied skill. It also could have positioned the film as a pioneer in inclusive stunt casting, especially in a genre that rarely features disabled performers.
Name: Sofia Boutella

Description: Blair Underwood was cast as Ironside in Ironside (2013 reboot). Ironside is a paraplegic detective, using a wheelchair after being shot in the line of duty. His disability is permanent and central to his investigative style.He’s portrayed as tough, brilliant, and emotionally guarded. The show attempts to modernise the 1967 original, focusing on psychological depth and procedural grit. Underwood is not disabled, and the casting drew criticism from disability advocates and actors. The reboot was cancelled after three episodes, partly due to backlash over inauthentic representation. Authentic casting could have redefined the procedural genre, showing a disabled lead navigating crime, trauma, and team dynamics with real-world insight. It would have reshaped relationships with colleagues and suspects, offering audiences a fresh lens on authority and embodiment. Publicity around inclusive casting could have positioned NBC as a leader in representation, rather than a cautionary tale.
Name: Blair Underwood

Description: François Cluzet cast as Philippe in Untouchable (2011). Philippe is a quadriplegic, paralysed from the neck down after a paragliding accident. He uses a motorised wheelchair and requires full-time care. Philippe is central to the film’s emotional arc. A wealthy man who forms an unlikely bond with his caregiver, Driss. Their relationship challenges social and cultural boundaries, with disability framed as a context for connection, not limitation. Cluzet is not disabled, and while the film is based on a true story, the casting choice maintains a non-disabled lens. The performance, though sensitive, lacks the embodied nuance of lived experience. Authentic casting would have reframed Philippe’s interactions, especially moments of intimacy, frustration, and humour as genuinely relational, not performed.
Name: François Cluzet

Description: William Hurt cast as Captain Ahab in Moby Dick (2011 miniseries). Ahab is a well know fictional character who is an amputee. Ahab is a below-the-knee amputee, having lost his leg to the white whale. He uses a prosthetic made of whalebone, which becomes a symbol of his obsession. Ahab’s disability is central to his identity, fuelling his vengeance and shaping his leadership. It’s not incidental; it’s metaphorical, representing trauma, obsession, and defiance. Hurt does not have a physical disability, and the role leans heavily on symbolic disability, where the impairment serves narrative metaphor rather than character depth.  Authentic casting could have grounded Ahab’s physicality—his gait, his pain, his presence—in real-world embodiment, reframing his relationships with Starbuck, Ishmael, and the crew. It would have added layers of credibility and challenged the tradition of casting disability as metaphor rather than experience.
Name: William Hurt

Description: Sam Claflin cast as Will Traynor in Me Before You (2016). Will is a quadriplegic, paralyzed from the neck down after a motorcycle accident. He uses a wheelchair and requires assistance with all daily tasks. Will’s story centers on his decision to pursue assisted suicide, despite developing a romantic relationship with his caregiver. His disability is portrayed as a life not worth living. Claflin is not disabled, and the film has been widely condemned for its ableist messaging. Authentic casting would have radically altered the film’s tone—offering a portrayal rooted in agency, complexity, and lived experience. It would have reframed Will’s relationships, especially with Louisa, as mutual and evolving, rather than tragic and one-sided. Publicity around authentic casting could have shifted the narrative from controversy to advocacy, positioning the film as a turning point in disability representation.
Name: Sam Claflin

Description: Jake Gyllenhaal cast as Jeff Bauman in Stronger (2017). Jeff Bauman is a double amputee and wheelchair user, injured in the Boston Marathon bombing. His recovery involves extensive physical and emotional adaptation. The film follows Jeff’s journey from trauma to resilience, focusing on his relationships, identity, and public visibility as a survivor. Gyllenhaal is not disabled, and while the performance is emotionally rich, it remains a simulation. Authentic casting would have transformed Jeff’s portrayal, especially in scenes of physical therapy, intimacy, and public scrutiny, into embodied truth. It would have reframed his relationship with Erin and his family as visibly authentic, challenging audiences to engage with disability as lived reality. Given the film’s real-life basis and awards campaign, authentic casting would have created a powerful publicity moment around survivor-led storytelling.
Name: Jake Gyllenhaal

Description: Grant Rosenmeyer cast as Scotty in Come as You Are (2019). Scotty is a wheelchair user with a congenital condition. He requires full-time mobility support and assistance with daily tasks. Scotty is the instigator of the road trip to a brothel catering to disabled clients. His character is brash, funny, and emotionally guarded, driving much of the film’s energy and conflict. Rosenmeyer is not disabled, and his casting—alongside producing the film—was widely criticised for cripping-up a role based on real disabled experiences.  Authentic casting would have transformed Scotty’s interactions with his mother, friends, and caregiver into visibly lived relationships, not performed ones. Audiences would recognise the authenticity in his frustration, humour, and vulnerability, reframing the film’s emotional arc. The film’s Sundance premiere and digital release could have been a publicity milestone for disability-led cinema, rather than a flashpoint for exclusion, and the statements released after it received bad publicity illustrated how uninformed the production was about how the disabled community feel about cripping-up.
Name: Grant Rosenmeyer

Description: Ravi Patel as Mo in Come As You Are (2019). Mo is the most cautious of the trio, often acting as the moral compass. His blindness is portrayed as a barrier to independence, but also a source of insight and empathy. Patel is not blind, and the role involves mimicking visual impairment. Critics noted that Mo’s blindness was often played for comic effect, undermining the character’s dignity, whereas a blind actor making the same jokes invites an audience to laugh with rather than laugh at the disabled character.  Authentic casting would have allowed Mo’s sensory navigation, emotional nuance, and interpersonal dynamics to emerge from real-world experience, not imitation. This would have reshaped his relationships with Scotty and Matt, especially in moments of tension and trust, making them recognisably authentic. The film’s message about disabled sexuality would have landed with greater credibility and impact if the casting had been authentic. Instead the film has aged quickly.
Name: Ravi Patel

Description: Hayden Szeto as Matt in Come As you Are (2019). Matt is a newly disabled wheelchair user following a spinal injury. He’s adjusting to life with paralysis and grappling with identity, intimacy, and self-worth. Matt is the emotional core of the film. His vulnerability and growth anchor the group’s journey. His disability is central to his arc, especially in scenes of therapy, frustration, and romantic interest. Szeto is not disabled, and his portrayal, though sensitive, remains a simulation bringing with it a feeling that it is out of step with the ethics of inclusion. Authentic casting would have reframed Matt’s physicality, emotional processing, and romantic tension as embodied truth. His relationship with the nurse driver and the other men would shift from scripted empathy to mutual recognition, allowing audiences to witness real disabled masculinity. The film’s exploration of disabled sexuality would have gained depth and legitimacy, especially in advocacy circles.
Name: Hayden Szeto

Description: Dwayne Johnson as Will Sawyer in Skyscraper (2018). Sawyer is a below-the-knee amputee, using a prosthetic leg for mobility and combat. His disability is the result of a traumatic rescue mission. Sawyer is the film’s action hero, rescuing his family from a burning skyscraper while navigating physical limitations. His prosthetic is used in stunts and emotional beats. Johnson is not an amputee, and the casting drew criticism from disabled actors and advocates, including Paralympian Katy Sullivan, who called it a missed opportunity for authentic representation. The film treats Sawyer’s disability as a superhuman enhancement, rather than a lived reality. Authentic casting would have reshaped Sawyer’s relationship with his family, his environment, and the audience, grounding heroism in real-world embodiment. It also would have positioned Universal Pictures as a leader in inclusive blockbuster casting, rather than a target of backlash.
Name: Dwayne Johnson

Description: Jason Momoa cast as Baba Voss in See (2019). Baba Voss is blind, like most characters in the post-apocalyptic world of See. His blindness is congenital or acquired early, and he navigates terrain, combat, and relationships without sight. He is the central protagonist, a warrior, father, and protector. His blindness is normalised, not emphasised, and his physicality challenges assumptions about disabled masculinity and leadership. Momoa is not blind. While praised for his physical performance, his portrayal relies on stylised movement and combat choreography rather than lived experience. Authentic casting would have reshaped Baba Voss’s relationships, especially with his children and Maghra, through recognisable embodiment, allowing audiences to witness real blind navigation, intimacy, and authority. The show’s use of a blind consultant helped mitigate misrepresentation, but the absence of disabled actors in lead roles was a missed opportunity for inclusive heroism.
Name: Jason Momoa

Description: Sylvia Hoeks cast as Queen Kane in See (2019). Queen Kane is blind, like most of her kingdom. Her blindness is part of the cultural norm, not a source of limitation. She is the antagonist, ruthless, manipulative, and politically dominant. Her blindness is not central to her villainy, but it informs her spiritual and authoritarian worldview.  Hoeks is not blind. Her portrayal leans into theatricality, with stylised gestures and vocal intensity. Authentic casting could have reframed Queen Kane’s power dynamics, especially her control over Tamacti Jun and Maghra, as embodied authority, not performed menace. It would have challenged the audience’s perception of disabled leadership, offering a rare portrayal of disabled political agency.
Name: Sylvia Hoeks

Description: Hera Hilmar cast as Maghra in See (2019).  Maghra is blind, though her children are sighted. Her blindness is culturally normalized, and she functions as a mother, strategist, and eventual queen. She is the emotional and political bridge between Baba Voss and Queen Kane. Her blindness is not a barrier, it’s part of her wisdom and resilience. Hilmar is not blind. Her performance emphasises grace and intuition, but lacks the physical nuance of blind embodiment. Authentic casting would have reshaped Maghra’s maternal and political relationships, especially with her sighted children, through visible authenticity, allowing audiences to engage with disability as lived experience, not symbolic wisdom. The show’s commitment to blindness training was commendable, but casting choices limited its representational impact.
Name: Hera Hilmar

Description: Christian Camargo cast as Tamacti Jun in See (2019). Tamacti Jun is blind, serving as Witchfinder General. His blindness is integrated into his tactical and moral evolution. Initially a ruthless enforcer, Jun becomes a reluctant ally. His blindness is portrayed as compatible with military strategy and emotional depth. Camargo is not blind. His portrayal is praised for complexity, but remains a performance. Authentic casting could have reframed Jun’s transformation from enforcer to ally as visibly grounded, allowing audiences to witness blind tactical reasoning and emotional vulnerability. It would have deepened his relationships with Maghra and Queen Kane, and the audience, shifting them from scripted tension to embodied negotiation.
Name: Christian Camargo

Description: Olivia Cheng cast as Charlotte in See (2019). Charlotte is blind, like most characters in the See universe. Her blindness is culturally normalised, and she navigates the world through sound, touch, and spatial awareness. Charlotte is a fierce warrior and protector of the Alkenny tribe. Her character is outspoken, loyal, and physically capable, challenging assumptions about disabled femininity and strength. Cheng is not blind. While her performance emphasises confidence and combat skill, it lacks the embodied nuance of blind navigation. Authentic casting could have reshaped Charlotte’s relationships through recognisable authenticity, allowing audiences to witness real blind spatial awareness and emotional depth. This would have elevated her role from warrior to embodied leader, enhancing both narrative and audience connection.
Name: Olivia Cheng

Description: Eden Epstein cast as Wren in See (2019). Wren is blind and serves as a Trivantian soldier and later a captain. Her blindness is integrated into her tactical and emotional intelligence. Wren is a key figure in the political and romantic arc of the series. Her relationship with Haniwa, a sighted character, explores trust, intimacy, and cultural difference. Epstein is not blind. Her portrayal of Wren’s emotional vulnerability and strategic thinking is compelling, but the lack of authentic casting limits the physical realism of her interactions. Authentic casting would have reframed Wren and Haniwa’s relationship, especially in moments of intimacy and conflict, as visibly mutual, not performative. This would have deepened the audience’s understanding of blind embodiment in romantic and military contexts, offering a rare portrayal of disabled queer identity.
Name: Eden Epstein

Description: Tom Mison cast as Lord Harlan in See (2019). Lord Harlan is blind and serves as the ruler of Pennsa. His blindness is part of the cultural norm, and he governs through diplomacy, charisma, and strategic alliances. Harlan is a political operator, cunning, charming, and often manipulative. His blindness is not emphasised but is part of his social navigation and authority. Mison is not blind. His performance leans into verbal dexterity and aristocratic flair, but lacks the embodied realism of leadership though a disabled person's lens. Authentic casting could have reframed Harlan’s power dynamics, especially with Maghra and Queen Kane, as visibly grounded, allowing audiences to engage with disabled authority and lived experience.
Name: Tom Mison

Description: Alfre Woodard cast as Paris in See (2019). Paris is blind and serves as the spiritual leader and matriarch of the Alkenny tribe. Her blindness is culturally normalised and informs her wisdom and intuition. Paris is a guide, healer, and emotional anchor. She supports Baba Voss and Maghra, offering insight and stability in times of crisis. Woodard is not blind. Her portrayal is emotionally rich and grounded, but the lack of authentic casting limits the physical credibility of her spiritual presence. Authentic casting would have reframed Paris’s mentorship and healing practices as embodied wisdom, not symbolic intuition. This would have deepened her relationships with the tribe and the audience, positioning her as a disabled elder whose authority is lived, not imagined. The difference is creatively subtle but potentially more interesting to the audience.
Name: Alfre Woodard

Description: Martin Roach cast as Captain Gosset in See (2019). Gosset is blind, like nearly all characters in See. His blindness is normalised within the world and does not hinder his role as a military commander. Gosset is a high-ranking officer in the Payan military, responsible for enforcing Queen Kane’s rule and preparing for war. He is authoritative, strategic, and politically aware. Roach is not blind. While his performance conveys command and discipline, it lacks the embodied realism of blind or disabled leadership. Authentic casting would have reframed Gosset’s authority. His interactions with Queen Kane and the Council would gain new depth, showing how disabled leaders navigate power structures. This would have challenged audience assumptions about disability and capability.
Name: Martin Roach

Description: Yadira Guevara-Prip cast as Bow Lion in See (2019). Bow Lion is blind and known as “The Shadow,” a stealth operative with exceptional sensory awareness. Her blindness is integral to her identity and skillset. She is a loyal ally to Baba Voss and a key figure in the Alkenny tribe’s survival. Her role blends espionage, spirituality, and combat. Guevara-Prip is not blind. Her portrayal emphasises grace and intensity, but not the physicality of blind stealth. Authentic casting would have transformed Bow Lion’s presence, especially in scenes of movement, silence, and touch, into visibly grounded action. Her bond with Baba Voss would shift from scripted loyalty to mutual recognition, allowing audiences to witness disabled embodiment as strength. This could have positioned Bow Lion as a landmark character in genre television.
Name: Yadira Guevara-Prip

Description: David Hewelett cast as Tormada in See (2019). Tormada is blind and serves as the Trivantian military’s chief scientist. His blindness is not emphasised visually but is part of the world’s baseline. Tormada is a villainous genius, developing weapons of mass destruction and orchestrating large-scale attacks. He is articulate, manipulative, and ideologically driven. Hewlett is not blind. His portrayal leans into theatrical intellect, but lacks embodied nuance. Authentic casting would have reframed Tormada’s menace, not as a stylised eccentricity, but as lived complexity. His interactions with allies and enemies would gain new texture, showing how a blind scientists could operate through non-visual cognition and tactile innovation. This would challenge stereotypes and elevate the character’s credibility.
Name: David Hewlett
Known For: Guillermo del Toro's Cabinet of Curiosities

Description: Hoon Lee cast as Toad in See (2019). Toad is blind, like most characters in See. His blindness is culturally normalised and does not impede his role as a skilled Witchfinder and protector. Toad is a loyal soldier tasked with escorting key characters. He evolves from a rigid enforcer to a compassionate ally, especially in his bond with Kofun. His blindness is portrayed as compatible with combat, strategy, and emotional growth. Lee is not blind. While his performance is compelling, it remains a simulation of blind embodiment. Authentic casting would have reshaped Toad’s mentorship and combat scenes.
Name: Hoon Lee

Description: Michael Raymond-James cast as Ranger in See (2019). Ranger is blind, like most characters in the series. His blindness is normalised and integrated into his survivalist lifestyle. Ranger is a nomadic warrior and ally to Baba Voss. He brings levity, resourcefulness, and emotional depth to the final season, especially in scenes of camaraderie and sacrifice. Raymond-James is not blind. His portrayal emphasises charm and agility, but lacks the physical nuance a blind actor could have brought to the role. Authentic casting would have reframed Ranger’s bond with Baba Voss, showing how blind warriors communicate, move, and connect both physically and emotionally. This would have elevated the show’s credibility and challenged assumptions about disabled masculinity. While Ranger was a fan favourite, however the casting choice continued the pattern in the show of sighted actors dominating blind roles.
Name: Michael Raymond-James

Description: Dave Bautista cast as Edo Voss in See (2019). Edo Voss is blind, like most characters in the See universe. His blindness is not emphasised visually but is part of the world’s baseline. Edo is the antagonist and brother of Baba Voss. He commands the Trivantian army and represents ideological opposition. His arc explores vengeance, power, and familial tension. Bautista is not blind. His performance is physically commanding, but the portrayal lacks embodied realism. Authentic casting would have reframed Edo’s rivalry with Baba Voss, allowing audiences to engage with disabled leadership as lived experience, not stylised menace. The show’s production team acknowledged the lack of blind actors as a gap, despite consulting with blindness experts.
Name: Dave Bautista

Description: Bruno Bichir cast as Dr Niles Caulder AKA The Chief in Titans (2018). Caulder is a wheelchair user, a brilliant scientist who assembles the Doom Patrol. His disability is permanent and central to his identity. He is a mentor and moral anchor, guiding superpowered individuals through trauma and transformation. His wheelchair use is visible and symbolic of his resilience and intellect. Bichir is not disabled. His portrayal is thoughtful, but the role remains a performance. Authentic casting would have transformed Caulder’s mentorship, especially in scenes of emotional vulnerability and scientific authority. It would have reframed his relationships with the Doom Patrol as visibly mutual, not hierarchical. The casting drew criticism from disability advocates, especially given the character’s iconic status in DC lore.
Name: Bruno Bichir

Description: Alec Baldwin was cast as Bill Oakland in Blind (2016). Bill Oakland is a novelist who becomes blind following a car accident. His vision loss is sudden and traumatic, and he relies on others for reading and mobility. Oakland is portrayed as emotionally closed off until he forms a bond with Suzanne, a woman assigned to read to him as part of her community service. Their relationship is framed as redemptive and romantic, with blindness as a barrier to overcome. Baldwin does not have a vision impairment, and the casting drew significant backlash from disability advocates. The Ruderman Family Foundation publicly condemned the film, comparing Baldwin’s performance to “crip-face” and calling it a form of exclusion. Authentic casting would have reframed Oakland’s emotional arc, not as a stylized performance of loss, but as embodied resilience. His relationship with Suzanne could have shifted from symbolic healing to mutual recognition, allowing audiences to engage with disability as lived experience. The film’s credibility and cultural impact would have been stronger with a blind actor in the lead.
Name: Alec Baldwin

Description: Blake Lively was cast as Gina, a young woman with a vision impairment in the movie All I See Is You (2016). Gina is a young woman who is blind due to a childhood accident. She regains partial sight through surgery, which alters her perception of her marriage and identity. The film explores Gina’s psychological transformation as she transitions from dependence to autonomy. Her restored vision reveals emotional and relational imbalances, especially with her controlling husband. Lively does not have a vision impairment, and her portrayal relies on visual stylization rather than embodied realism. While the film attempts to explore sensory experience, it does so through a non-disabled lens, missing the opportunity to depict real-world navigation, intimacy, and autonomy. Authentic casting would have transformed Gina’s journey, especially her shifting relationship with her husband, into visibly grounded emotional evolution. It would have challenged audience assumptions about disabled femininity and agency, offering a richer portrayal of identity and desire.
Name: Blake Lively

Description: Eileen Walsh was cast as Catherine Proctor in Small Town, Big Story (2025). Catherine Proctor is a wheelchair user in a small Irish town. Her mobility impairment is permanent and visible, though details of its origin are not central to the plot. She is a key figure in the community, involved in the unfolding drama when a Hollywood production descends on the town. Her role blends local authority, wit, and emotional depth. Walsh is not physically disabled, and while her performance is acclaimed, the casting continues the pattern of non-disabled actors portraying disabled characters. Authentic casting would have reshaped Catherine’s interactions, especially with her family and community, through recognisable embodiment, allowing audiences to engage with disability as part of everyday life, not just a surface narrative device. Given the show’s high-profile cast and Sky Studios backing and their commitment to disability inclusion, authentic casting could have been a publicity milestone for inclusive representation, positioning the series as a leader in disability visibility.
Name: Eileen Walsh

Description: Natalia Cordova-Buckley was cast as Yo-Yo Rodriguez AKA Slingshot in Yo-Yo Rodriguez in Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D. (2013 to 2020). Yo-Yo Rodriguez loses both arms in Season 5 and receives cybernetic prosthetics. Her disability is permanent and integrated into her powers and identity. This wouldn't have made it impossible for a disabled actor to play the role as the prosthetics are CGI-enhanced, which could be adapted for a disabled performer but would have required intentional design from the outset. Studios rarely recast mid-series, even when disability becomes central, however there are examples of where disabled actors have played non-disabled roles that then become disabled, and this could have been explored as Yo-Yo's preceding comic story has a similar story arc. Yo-Yo is a core member of the S.H.I.E.L.D. team, known for her super-speed and moral clarity. Her amputation is treated as a turning point, deepening her emotional resilience and tactical role. Cordova-Buckley is not an amputee or have any form of physical disability. While her portrayal is emotionally rich, the prosthetics are simulated, and the physicality of limb difference is not embodied. Authentic casting would have reshaped Yo-Yo’s relationships, especially with Mack and Daisy, through visible mutuality and trust, allowing audiences to engage with disabled heroism as lived experience.
Name: Natalia Cordova-Buckley

Description: Leslie Uggams cast as Blind Al in the Deadpool series.  Blind Al is blind, navigating her home with tactile familiarity and sharp wit. Her blindness is permanent and central to her identity and is also the core of a lot of her more comedic moments and interactions. Al is Deadpool’s roommate and confidante, offering comic relief and emotional grounding. Her blindness is normalised, not pitied, and she’s portrayed as independent and assertive. Uggams is not vision impaired. While her performance is beloved, the role remains an uncomfortable simulation. Authentic casting would have reframed Al’s bond with Wade Wilson as visibly reciprocal, challenging stereotypes about disabled elders and deepening the emotional texture of their domestic scenes. The character’s popularity could have been a publicity milestone for disability visibility, but the casting choice kept the portrayal within a non-disabled lens.
Name: Leslie Uggams

Description: Jon Cryer cast as Lex Luthour in Supergirl (2015 to 2021). Lex becomes a wheelchair user due to cancer-related complications. His disability is visible and affects his mobility, though not his intellect or ambition. Lex is the central antagonist manipulative, brilliant, and ideologically driven. His disability is part of his arc but not the source of his villainy. Cryer does not have a physical mobility disability. While his performance was praised, the wheelchair use was mimicked, not embodied.  Authentic casting would have reframed Lex’s power dynamics, especially with Lena and Supergirl, as grounded in lived experience, showing how disabled intellect operates within systems of control. The show missed a chance to challenge the tradition of disabled villains being portrayed by non-disabled actors, especially in a franchise with wide reach and cultural impact.
Name: Jon Cryer

Description: Ludi Lin cast as Captain Murk in Aquaman (2018).  In the comics, Murk is a one-armed Atlantean warrior, using a blade prosthetic. His disability is visible and central to his combat identity. In the film, Murk is reimagined as a two-armed enforcer for King Orm. His comic book disability is erased, and the character is portrayed as physically dominant and loyal. Lin is not disabled, and the film removed Murk’s amputation entirely. This is a clear case of disability erasure. Authentic casting and retention of Murk’s limb difference would have reshaped his combat scenes and loyalty dynamics, offering audiences a disabled warrior whose strength is not despite his disability but through it. The film’s global success could have amplified disability representation, but instead sidelined it.
Name: Ludi Lin

Description: Brenton Thwaites was cast as a double amputee Nic in The Signal (2014). Nic is a double amputee following an unexplained trauma. He uses a wheelchair early in the film and later discovers he has been fitted with advanced prosthetics, which become central to the sci-fi twist. Nic is the protagonist, navigating confusion, betrayal, and transformation. His disability is initially framed as a limitation, then re-contextualised as a gateway to power and escape. Thwaites is not a wheelchair user and does not have a physical disability, and the role involves wheelchair use,  physical disability embodiment and related psychological trauma. The film’s genre framing, sci-fi thriller, leans into disability as mystery, rather than lived experience. Authentic casting would have grounded Nic’s emotional arc, especially in scenes of frustration, intimacy, and discovery. His relationships with Haley and Jonah would shift from stylised empathy to recognisable mutuality, allowing audiences to engage with disability as part of identity, not just plot mechanics. Despite its Sundance premiere, the film missed a chance to lead in inclusive genre storytelling.
Name: Brenton Thwaites
Known For: Pirates of the Caribbean: Dead Men Tell No Tales

Description: Michael Emerson was cast as an amputee Wilzig in Fallout (2024). Dr. Siggi Wilzig is an amputee with a prosthetic limb, portrayed as a soft-spoken scientist and fugitive. His disability is visible and tied to his survival in the post-apocalyptic world. Wilzig is a key figure in the series’ lore, connected to cold fusion technology and Lucy MacLean’s journey. His arc blends mystery, sacrifice, and legacy. Emerson is not disabled. While his performance is praised for nuance, the prosthetic is simulated, and the embodiment of disability is absent. Authentic casting would have reshaped Wilzig’s mentorship and fugitive status, allowing audiences to witness disabled survival and scientific authority as lived experience. His relationship with Lucy would gain emotional depth, reframing trust and vulnerability. The show’s high-profile release on Prime Video sparked some online debate, but no major backlash, though disability advocates noted the missed opportunity for authentic representation in a prestige series.
Name: Michael Emerson

Description: Caleb Landry Jones was cast as wheelchair user Doug Monroe in DogMan (2023). Doug is a wheelchair user, abused by his father and raised with dogs. His disability is permanent and central to his isolation, identity, and emotional resilience. Doug is the film’s protagonist, a traumatised antihero who finds solace in his canine companions and cabaret performances. His disability is portrayed as part of his survival and creative expression. Jones is not a wheelchair user or physically disabled. His performance is stylised, blending drag, trauma, and eccentricity. While praised for intensity, it remains a simulation. Authentic casting would have reframed Doug’s relationships with the dogs, the therapist, and the audience as visibly embodied and emotionally grounded. The film’s surreal tone could have been anchored by real-world disability experience, offering a rare portrayal of disabled queer masculinity. Despite its Venice premiere, the film drew criticism from some disability advocates for its casting and stylisation.
Name: Caleb Landry Jones

Description: Lorenzo James Henrie was cast as Gabe Reyes in Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D. (2014). Gabe is a wheelchair user and uses crutches due to a spinal condition. His disability is permanent and affects his mobility and independence. In the comics he is also an ambulant wheelchair user. Gabe is the younger brother of Robbie Reyes (Ghost Rider). His disability is part of Robbie’s motivation and emotional grounding. Gabe is portrayed as supportive, intelligent, and emotionally complex. Henrie is not disabled. While Gabe’s portrayal avoids pity, it remains a cripped-up performance. Authentic casting would have reshaped Gabe’s bond with Robbie, especially in scenes of protection, conflict, and vulnerability. Audiences would recognise the authenticity of disabled sibling-hood, reframing their dynamic as mutual and embodied. The show’s progressive casting elsewhere made this omission more noticeable.
Name: Lorenzo James Henrie

Description: Gabe White was cast as disabled wheelchair user Aaron James in The Defenders (2017). Aaron James is a wheelchair user following exposure to a toxic chemical. His disability is permanent and affects his mobility and emotional wellbeing. Aaron is a client of Matt Murdock, seeking justice for his injury. His scenes explore anger, loss, and the legal system’s failure to protect disabled people. Gabe White is not disabled. Authentic casting would have reframed Aaron’s relationship with Matt Murdock, shifting it from scripted empathy to mutual recognition. Audiences would engage more deeply with Aaron’s frustration and agency, especially in scenes of legal advocacy. The show missed a chance to model authentic disabled representation in a grounded, contemporary setting.
Name: Gabe White

Description: Anjelika Washington was cast as Beth Chapel AKA Doctor Mid-Nite in Stargirl, (2020 to 2022). Beth Chapel inherits the mantle of Doctor Mid-Nite, a legacy character originally blind. In the comics, Beth uses enhanced goggles to see in darkness, aligning her with low-vision or blind-coded traits. In the comics Beth was blinded in an accident during her medical internship, raising concerns about disability identity erasure between page and screen and removing the opportunity to cast authentically. Beth is a tech-savvy, optimistic member of the Justice Society. Her arc centers on friendship, courage, and stepping into leadership. Washington is not blind or has a vision impairment, and the show reimagines Beth as sighted. This is a case of disability erasure, where a canonically disabled character is rewritten without their impairment. Authentic casting and retention of Beth’s blindness would have reshaped her relationships with Courtney and Rick, allowing audiences to witness disabled heroism as lived experience. It would have positioned Stargirl as a leader in inclusive superhero storytelling, especially given its youth audience and progressive tone
Name: Anjelika Washington

Description: Boyd Holbrook was cast as Pierce AKA White Bishop, in the movie Logan (2017). Pierce is a cyborg with multiple cybernetic limbs and enhancements. In the comics, he is a disabled human who augments his body to gain power and mobility, and is a disability icon. Pierce is the film’s antagonist, a bounty hunter leading the Reavers. His cybernetics are visual markers of menace and control, and these are a lot more prominent in the original text. Holbrook is does not have a physical disability, and the film stylizes Pierce’s enhancements without exploring their origin or embodiment. Authentic casting would have reframed Pierce’s interactions with Logan and Laura, grounding his menace in real-world disability experience rather than stylized augmentation. The film’s gritty tone could have supported a more complex portrayal of disabled villainy. Critics noted the flattening of Pierce’s comic backstory, missing a chance to explore disability and power, and what was left was a one dimensional characterisation of disability.
Name: Boyd Holbrook

Description: Daniel Bernhardt was cast as Bonebreaker in Logan (2017). Bonebreaker is a cyborg with a tank-like lower body and extensive limb differences. In the comics, he is a disabled mercenary who uses mobility-enhancing tech. In Logan, Bonebreaker is a minor Reaver enforcer. His physicality is stylized but lacks the distinct disability identity of the comics. Bernhardt is not physically disabled, and the film reduces Bonebreaker’s disability to visual flair. Authentic casting and faithful adaptation of Bonebreaker’s mobility tech would have reshaped his combat scenes and team dynamics, offering audiences a disabled warrior whose strength is not despite his impairment but through it. The erasure of his disability identity—alongside Pretty Boy—was noted by fans as a dilution of the Reavers’ original narrative complexity.
Name: Daniel Bernhardt

Description: Blake Ritson was cast as Brainiac in Krypton (2018 to 2019). In the comics, Brainiac is a Coluan alien whose body is extensively cybernetic. His enhancements are not just aesthetic, they replace organic function, making him a canonical disabled character reliant on assistive technology. In Krypton, Brainiac is the central antagonist, a collector of worlds and embodiment of cold logic. His cybernetics are stylised as alien superiority rather than disability. Ritson is not physically disabled, and the show reframes Brainiac’s cybernetics as menace, not embodiment. This removes the opportunity to explore disabled intelligence, power and autonomy. Authentic casting could have reframed Brainiac’s interactions with Seg-El and the Voice of Rao as embodied power, especially in scenes of control, surveillance, and philosophical debate.
Name: Blake Ritson

Description: Freddy Carter was cast as Kaz Brekker in Shadow and Bone (2021 to 2023). Kaz is a cane user due to a leg injury sustained in childhood. His disability is permanent and affects his mobility, pain levels, and emotional regulation. Kaz is a gang leader and strategist. His disability shapes his physicality and emotional armour, especially in scenes of intimacy and trauma. Carter is not physically disabled, and while the show retains Kaz’s cane use, it lacks embodied realism. Critics and fans noted the absence of pain, fatigue, and adaptive movement. Authentic casting would have reshaped Kaz’s relationships, especially with Inej and Jesper, allowing audiences to engage with disabled masculinity as lived experience.
Name: Freddy Carter

Description: Kyriana Kratter was cast as KB in Star Wars: Skeleton Crew (2024 to 2025). KB is a disabled child with cybernetic assistive technologies (“augs”) that support her mobility, cognition, and survival. Her disability identity is central to her arc, including scenes of tech failure and emotional vulnerability. KB is part of a young crew navigating survival and belonging. Her disability is portrayed with nuance, affecting her decisions, relationships, and self-perception. Kratter is not physically disabled, though her performance has been praised for emotional depth. Critics noted that KB’s portrayal centred disabled agency, but the casting still reflects a non-disabled lens. Authentic casting would have reframed KB’s bond with Fern and Wim as recognisably embodied, especially in the more fearful emotional scenes that include medical urgency and tech dependence.  This was a missed opportunity for inclusive casting and storytelling which seems at odds with Disney's creative ethos.
Name: Kyriana Kratter

Description: Maddie Ziegler was cast as Music in the movie Music (2021). Music is a non-verbal autistic teenager. Her disability is central to the plot, which explores guardianship, routine, and sensory experience. Music is the emotional anchor of the film, but her perspective is sidelined in favour of her sister’s redemption arc. Her autism is stylized through choreography and exaggerated facial expressions. Ziegler is not neurodivergent, and the film was widely condemned for ableist portrayal. Critics and advocacy groups including the Autistic Self Advocacy Network, called the performance offensive and harmful. Sia’s defence and later apology drew further backlash. Authentic casting would have transformed Music’s relationships, especially with Zu and Ebo, into mutual, embodied care, rather than stylised burden. The film’s Golden Globe nomination intensified criticism, making it a case study in failed representation
Name: Maddie Ziegler

Description: Edan Hayhurst was cast as Colin in A Secret Garden (2020). A literary character that is recognised as physically disabled. Colin is a child with a physical disability, often interpreted as a spinal condition or psychosomatic paralysis. He uses a wheelchair and is confined indoors due to fears about his health. Colin’s arc centres on transformation: from isolation and fragility to emotional and physical awakening through friendship and nature. His disability is a metaphor for repression and healing. Hayhurst is not physically disabled. While the performance is sensitive, it still has all the hallmarks of simulation rather than embodiment. Authentic casting would have reframed Colin’s bond with Mary Lennox, allowing audiences to witness disabled childhood as lived experience, not symbolic recovery.  Critics have long debated Colin’s portrayal across adaptations, with some noting the tendency to “cripple for narrative effect”. Authentic casting could have shifted the lens from metaphor to embodiment, especially in scenes of movement, frustration, and joy.
Name: Edan Hayhurst

Description: James McAvoy was cast as Charles Xavier in X-Men: Dark Phoenix (2019), X-Men: Apocalypse (2016), X-Men: Days of Future Past (2014) and X-Men: First Class (2011). Charles Xavier is a wheelchair user following a spinal injury. His disability is permanent and central to his identity as a leader and telepath. Xavier is the founder of the X-Men, a mentor and strategist. His disability is visible but rarely explored emotionally; it’s treated as incidental to his powers and intellect. McAvoy is not a wheelchair user or physically disabled. While the performance is iconic, the wheelchair use is mimicked, and the physicality and biases needs to be overcome as part of disabled leadership is absent.
