Authentic casting would have reshaped Xavier’s mentorship and relationships, especially with Magneto and Jean Grey, as grounded in lived experience, challenging stereotypes and biases about disabled authority. The franchise’s reliance on non-disabled actors (including Patrick Stewart) has sparked ongoing debate.
Name: James McAvoy

Description: Levente Puczkó-Smith was cast as the physically disabled boy Ruben in Midsommer (2019). Ruben is a non-verbal, physically disabled child with facial differences, portrayed as the cult’s oracle. His disability is congenital and tied to inbreeding within the community. Ruben is a symbolic figure used to justify ritual and prophecy. He does not speak or interact meaningfully, and his drawings are interpreted by elders. Puczkó-Smith is not physically disabled. The portrayal sparked significant backlash for using disability as horror aesthetic. Critics called it exploitative and dehumanizing. Authentic casting could have challenged this framing, offering a portrayal of disabled spirituality and agency rather than mystification. His presence could have been reframed as embodied wisdom, not eerie spectacle.
Name: Levente Puczkó-Smith

Description: Annarah Cymone was cast as Leeza Scarborough in Midnight Mass (2021). Leeza is a wheelchair user due to a spinal injury. Her disability is permanent until a supernatural event restores her ability to walk. Leeza is a moral and emotional anchor, her forgiveness of the man who shot her is a pivotal moment. Her healing is framed as miraculous and symbolic of faith. Cymone is not a wheelchair user or physically disabled. While her performance is emotionally compelling, the role centres on disability as something to be cured. Authentic casting would have grounded her story in real disabled embodiment, allowing audiences to engage with faith, trauma, and agency through lived experience. The show received praise for its writing, but also criticism for its inappropriate casting choice.
Name: Annarah Cymone

Description: Kwesi Ameyaw was cast as Dr MidNight in Legends of Tomorrow (2016 to 2017). Dr. Mid-Nite (Charles McNider) is canonically blind in DC Comics, using specialised goggles to see in darkness. His blindness is central to his identity as a physician and superhero. In Legends of Tomorrow, Dr. Mid-Nite is a member of the Justice Society of America. His blindness is referenced but visually minimised through cybernetic enhancements, an assistive technology that effectively erases the physical and societal barriers he faces when he is not using them. Kwesi Ameyaw is not vision impaired. The show’s depiction of Dr. Mid-Nite leans into tech-enabled vision rather than blind embodiment.  Authentic casting would have reframed his interactions with the team as grounded in blind spatial awareness and lived experience, not enhancement. Missed creative opportunities such as exploring if he would perceive vision in the same way same as sighted people do, and how that would change his reliance on other senses and muscle memory, made this core aspect of is character less interesting, as it is disability from a non-disabled pespective. The erasure of his disability identity from screen adaptation undermines the character’s legacy as one of DC’s earliest disabled heroes.
Name: Kwesi Ameyaw

Description: Rhenzy Feliz was cast as Victor Aguilar in The Penguin (2025). Victor is portrayed with a stutter, a speech disability that affects fluency and verbal expression. The character’s stammer is introduced during casting, not scripted initially. Victor is a newly created character for HBO’s The Penguin, serving as Oz Cobb’s sidekick. His stutter adds emotional texture and vulnerability to his loyalty and courage. Feliz does not have a stutter. He expressed concern about portraying the trait authentically after it was introduced mid-audition. While the performance has been praised, disability advocates have raised questions about the lack of consultation and casting transparency. Authentic casting would have both reshaped Victor’s relationship with Oz and deepened it with the audience, offering a portrayal of speech and communication disability rooted in lived experience, not performance. It also would have positioned HBO as a leader in inclusive character creation.
Name: Rhenzy Feliz

Description: Kathleen Munroe was cast as Dr. Amanda Perry, a quadriplegic character, in the TV series Stargate Universe. Her character was part of an episode where Ming-Na's character, Camille Wray, used communication stones to inhabit Dr. Perry's body. Dr. Perry is a quadriplegic scientist, paralyzed from the neck down due to a childhood accident. Her disability is permanent and affects all aspects of her physical autonomy. Perry is a brilliant physicist whose consciousness is transferred to another body via alien technology. Her storyline explores identity, embodiment, and emotional connection, especially with Dr. Rush. Munroe is not a physically disabled actor. While the character is portrayed with dignity, the use of communication stones to “escape” her disabled body reinforces problematic ideas of disability as limitation. Authentic casting would have reframed Perry’s emotional arc, especially her intimacy with Rush, as grounded in disabled embodiment, not escapism. The episode sparked debate among fans and critics about the ethics of body-swapping narratives involving disabled characters, something that could have been successfully reframed with a disabled actor.
Name: Kathleen Munroe

Description: Lola Petticrew was cast as Tuesday in Tuesday (2023). Tuesday is a terminally ill teenager and wheelchair user. Her disability is central to the film’s emotional arc, which explores mortality, grief, and maternal love. Tuesday’s relationship with her mother (played by Julia Louis-Dreyfus) drives the narrative. Her disability is portrayed with sensitivity, but stylized through fantasy elements involving Death as a talking bird. Petticrew is not physically disabled. While the performance is emotionally resonant, the casting choice limits the film’s credibility in portraying disabled youth. Authentic casting would have reshaped and enriched Tuesday’s bond with her mother, especially in scenes of resistance, vulnerability, and acceptance.Critics praised the film’s ambition but noted the missed opportunity for disability-led storytelling.
Name: Lola Petticrew

Description: Christoph Waltz cast as Dr. Dyson Ido in Alita: Battle Angel (2019). In the original manga (Battle Angel Alita), Dr. Ido is depicted with a prosthetic arm, an explicit limb difference that aligns him with the cyborg population of Iron City. In the film adaptation, this aspect is visually minimized or removed, and Ido is portrayed as fully able-bodied. Ido is Alita’s surrogate father, a compassionate cyber-surgeon and part-time Hunter-Warrior. His emotional arc centers on grief, protection, and moral conflict. He repairs and upgrades cyborgs, including Alita, and serves as the audience’s guide into the world’s ethics and dangers. Waltz is not disabled, and the film adaptation erases Ido’s prosthetic identity. This is a clear case of disability erasure, where a canonically limb-different character is reimagined as non-disabled. Authentic casting would have reframed Ido’s relationship with Alita, not just as a caregiver, but as someone who shares her embodied experience, deepening their emotional bond and mutual recognition. Scenes of repair, mentorship, and grief would gain new texture if performed by an actor with lived experience of limb difference or prosthetic use. The erasure also undermines the film’s broader themes of body autonomy, augmentation, and survival. In a world where nearly every character is physically modified, the decision to cast a non-disabled actor and remove Ido’s prosthetic identity signals a reluctance to center disabled embodiment, even in a cybernetic context.
Name: Christoph Waltz

Description: Jackie Earle Haley cast as Grewishka in Alita: Battle Angel (2019). Grewishka is a heavily augmented cyborg with extreme body modifications, including prosthetic limbs and a mechanised torso. His original human form is almost entirely replaced with assistive technology.  He serves as a brutal enforcer for Nova, embodying menace and physical dominance. His augmentations are used to amplify threat and dehumanisation. Despite his disabilities without his technology being profound to the extreme, he does not experience barriers in his environment. The role leans into cybernetic monstrosity, reinforcing the idea that extensive prosthetics equal moral decay. Authentic casting would have reframed Grewishka’s rage and vulnerability, especially in his confrontations with Alita, as rooted in lived experience, not stylised horror. This could have offered a more complex emotional arc.
Name: Jackie Earle Haley

Description: Ed Skrein cast as Zapan in Alita: Battle Angel (2019). Zapan is a cyborg with a fully prosthetic body and a human face. His enhancements are sleek and stylized, emphasizing agility and vanity. He is a Hunter-Warrior and antagonist, driven by ego and revenge. His body is central to his identity and his rivalry with Alita. The role fetishizes prosthetics as aesthetic superiority, rather than functional embodiment. Authentic casting would have reshaped Zapan’s arrogance and downfall, especially in scenes of body loss and reconstruction, as emotionally grounded, not performative. His relationship with the Hunter-Warrior community could have reflected real disabled masculinity and status.
Name: Ed Skrein

Description: Eiza González cast as Nyssiana in Alita: Battle Angel (2019). Nyssiana is a cyborg with detachable limbs and a segmented body. Her augmentations allow her to disguise herself and attack with surprise. She is a sadistic assassin who lures victims into traps. Her body is weaponised and stylised for deception. The role uses the physical disability identity of limb difference as visual shock. Authentic casting would have reframed Nyssiana’s physicality and psychological complexity, allowing audiences to engage with disabled femininity as layered. Her brief but intense interaction with Alita could have carried deeper emotional resonance.
Name: Eiza González

Description: Casper Van Dien cast as Amok in Alita: Battle Angel (2019) Amok is a cyborg criminal with visible augmentations. His body is partially mechanised, though less stylised than other characters. The role is minor, but still contributes to the pattern of non-disabled actors portraying limb-different characters. Authentic casting, even in brief roles, would have signalled commitment to inclusive embodiment, allowing disabled performers to populate the world of Iron City with lived realism.
Name: Casper Van Dien

Description: Elle LaMont cast as Screwhead in Alita: Battle Angel (2019) Screwhead is a cyborg with a cranial-mounted weapon and visible prosthetics. Her body is designed for combat and intimidation. She is a Hunter-Warrior who fights Alita in the Kansas Bar. Her augmentations are central to her fighting style and identity. The role uses prosthetics as combat spectacle, not character depth. Authentic casting could have reframed Screwhead’s aggression and status as part of a lived disabled identity, challenging the idea that prosthetics are purely for violence, but agency and autonomy. Her brief but memorable presence could have been a lot more impactful with authentic casting.
Name: Elle LaMont

Description: Jeff Fahey cast as McTeague in Alita: Battle Angel (2019) McTeague is a cyborg with multiple prosthetic enhancements, including mechanical arms and sensory devices. He is a bounty hunter with a pack of cybernetic dogs. He is a peripheral but visually striking character, contributing to the film’s world-building and tension. The role stylises limb difference as eccentricity, missing the chance to explore disabled survival and companionship.
Name: Jeff Fahey

Description: Jacob Tremblay was cast in the movie Wonder (2017). Auggie is a 10-year-old boy with Treacher Collins syndrome, a craniofacial condition affecting bone and tissue development. He has undergone multiple surgeries and experiences social stigma due to his appearance. Auggie is the emotional core of the film. His journey through mainstream schooling explores bullying, friendship, and resilience. The story centers on empathy and acceptance. Tremblay is not disabled. His portrayal relied on prosthetic makeup, which critics argued softened the condition’s visual impact. Disability advocates condemned the casting as a missed opportunity for authentic representation, especially given the film’s message of inclusion. Authentic casting would have reframed Auggie’s relationships with his peers, teachers, and family, allowing audiences to engage with disabled childhood as lived truth, not stylised inspiration. Casting needn't have been disability literal as the syndrome is rare, but having a disabled actor with a visible difference playing the role could have added depths of understanding, and insight to the performance and connected better with disabled audiences.
Name: Jacob Tremblay

Description: Jamie Sives was cast as James Hardy in Department Q (2025). Hardy is a former police officer who becomes paraplegic after being shot. He uses a wheelchair and is portrayed as emotionally withdrawn and physically limited. Hardy’s disability is central to the mystery and emotional tension. His past is revealed slowly, and his trauma shapes the investigation’s stakes. Sives is not disabled. The role includes minimal pre-injury footage, raising concerns about faked embodiment as productions like Better (2022) have shown that with thoughtful direction, disabled actors can play pre-trauma characters. Authentic casting would have reshaped Hardy’s emotional arc, especially in scenes of regret, resilience, and confrontation as grounded in lived experience. It would also have deepened his relationship with the lead detectives and the audience, offering a portrayal of disabled masculinity rooted in truth.
Name: Jamie Sives

Description: David Bradley has been cast as the Blind Man (De Lacey in the novel) in the 2025 production of Frankenstein. De Lacey is blind and unable to perceive the Creature’s appearance. His blindness allows for a moment of unconditional acceptance, a rare human connection in the novel. He is the only character who treats the Creature with dignity, offering friendship and kindness. His role is pivotal in exploring themes of prejudice, empathy, and isolation. Bradley is not blind. The casting overlooks the opportunity to center disabled perception as moral clarity. Authentic casting would have reframed De Lacey’s relationship with the Creature as a shared experience of marginalisation. The scene’s power lies in its sincerity, something only lived experience can fully convey.
Name: David Bradley

Description: Elena Anaya was cast as Dr Maru in Wonder Woman (2017). Dr. Maru has severe facial differences, partially concealed by a prosthetic mask. Her condition is never named but is visually stylised. She is a chemist and antagonist, developing deadly weapons. Her facial difference is used to signal emotional instability, vulnerability and moral corruption. Anaya is not disabled. Critics noted that Maru’s condition was exploited as a weakness and aesthetic threat. Authentic casting could have challenged this framing, recasting Maru’s intelligence and ambition as rooted in disabled embodiment, not stylized menace. Her relationship with Ludendorff and Diana could have explored power, autonomy, and resistance through a disability lens, adding to her psychopathy a character who has also suffered isolation and prejudice.
Name: Elena Anaya

Description: Stephen Root was cast as Jim Hudson in the movie Get Out (2017), and also another blind character known as Radio Station Man in O Brother, Where Art Thou? (2000). Jim Hudson is blind due to a genetic condition, and Radio Station Man is also portrayed as blind. Both characters rely on auditory perception and tactile navigation. Jim Hudson is a seemingly sympathetic art dealer who ultimately bids on Chris’s body in the film’s organ-harvesting plot. His blindness is used to justify his desire for Chris’s eyes. In O Brother, Radio Station Man records the Soggy Bottom Boys, using his blindness as a comic and eccentric trait. Root is not vision impaired. In Get Out, his blindness is used as a plot device to mask villainy. In O Brother, blindness is played for laughs. Authentic casting would have reframed Jim’s scenes with Chris as emotionally grounded, especially in moments of betrayal and philosophical dialogue, allowing audiences to engage with disabled embodiment as truth, not twist.
Name: Stephen Root

Description: Bill Nighy was cast as Howard Clifford in the movie Pokémon: Detective Pikachu (2019). Clifford is a wheelchair user due to a degenerative disease. His disability is permanent and central to his motivations. Clifford is the film’s antagonist, seeking to merge human consciousness with Pokémon. His wheelchair use is visually emphasised, and his disability is framed as a limitation he seeks to overcome through unethical means. Nighy is not a wheelchair user nor is physically disabled. The film was criticised for poor disability portrayal. Authentic casting would have reframed Clifford’s ambition and emotional arc, especially his relationship with his son. The film’s global reach made this a missed opportunity for inclusive blockbuster storytelling.
Name: Bill Nighy

Description: Sally Hawkins was cast as Elisa Esposito in The Shape of Water (2017). Elisa is mute and communicates using American Sign Language (ASL). Her disability is congenital and central to her identity. Elisa is the film’s protagonist, a cleaner at a government facility who forms a romantic bond with a captive amphibian creature. Her muteness is portrayed as poetic and symbolic of emotional depth. Hawkins is not disabled and was not fluent in ASL prior to filming. Critics noted that her signing lacked authenticity and fluidity. Authentic casting would have reshaped Elisa’s relationships with Giles and the creature. The film won multiple Oscars, but disability advocates highlighted the erasure of disabled performers in a story about voice and otherness.
Name: Sally Hawkins

Description: Rosie Cavaliero was cast as Hesther in Hunderby (2012 to 2015).  Hesther is a wheelchair user in a period comedy setting. Her disability is permanent and used for visual contrast and comic tension. Her disability isn't scripted but is present simply through the incidental and persistent use if a wheelchair. Hesther is a supporting character whose mobility impairment is part of the show’s dark humour and gothic absurdity. Cavaliero is not a wheelchair user or physically disabled. Authentic casting would have reframed Hesther’s interactions with Helene and Dorothy as grounded in disabled embodiment, challenging the audience to see disability as character, not caricature. The show’s stylized tone made this a subtle but persistent form of exclusion.
Name: Rosie Cavaliero

Description: Michael Sheen was cast as Art Honeyman in the movie Music Within (2007). Art Honeyman was a real-life poet and activist with cerebral palsy. He used a wheelchair and had significant speech and motor impairments. In the film, Honeyman is portrayed as a witty, politically engaged figure who challenges social norms and becomes a close friend of the protagonist, Richard Pimentel. His disability is central to his activism and identity. Sheen is neither a wheelchair user nor has cerebral palsy. His portrayal involved mimicking physical traits and speech patterns, which many disability advocates criticised as cripping-up. Authentic casting would have reframed Honeyman’s scenes, especially those involving protest, friendship, and public confrontation, as rooted in lived experience. The emotional depth of his bond with Pimentel could have been more resonant and credible. While the film was praised for its message, it missed a key opportunity to model inclusive biopic casting.
Name: Michael Sheen

Description: Jonny Lee Miller was cast Lord Byron in the TV Movie called Byron (2003). Lord Byron had a clubfoot, a congenital condition affecting the structure and mobility of his foot. It caused him pain and affected his gait, movement and mobility throughout his life. Byron is portrayed as a romantic, rebellious poet whose physical and emotional intensity shaped his literary legacy. His disability is referenced but not central to the narrative. Miller is not disabled, and the portrayal largely omits Byron’s disability as a meaningful part of his identity. Authentic casting could have reframed Byron’s relationships with lovers, critics, and himself, as shaped by embodied difference, not just emotional turmoil. It would have added depth to his defiance and vulnerability, especially in scenes of exile and introspection. The absence of disability nuance reflects a broader pattern of disability erasure in period dramas.
Name: Jonny Lee Miller

Description: The actor won an academy award for his portrayal of blind musician Ray Charles in the movie Ray (2004). Ray Charles was blind from the age of seven due to glaucoma. His blindness was permanent and central to his musical style, independence, and public persona. Charles is the protagonist of the biopic, which explores his rise to fame, personal struggles, and artistic genius. His blindness is portrayed as both a challenge and a source of creative power. Foxx is not blind or vision impaired. While his performance won an Academy Award and was widely acclaimed, disability advocates noted that the role perpetuated the tradition of non-disabled actors portraying disabled icons. Authentic casting would have reshaped Charles’s relationships, with his band, family, and audience, as visibly grounded in disabled embodiment. The film’s emotional arc could have been enriched by lived experience, especially in scenes of isolation and resilience.
Name: Jamie Foxx

Description: William H. Macy was cast as salesman Bill Porter in the movie Door to Door (2002).  Bill Porter was a real-life salesman with cerebral palsy. His condition affected his speech, gait, and motor coordination, but he worked for decades as a door-to-door salesman. Porter is portrayed as determined, kind, and resilient. The film centers on his professional journey and personal dignity, positioning him as an inspirational figure. Macy is physically disabled or have palsy. His portrayal involved mimicking Porter’s physical traits, which drew criticism for performance over embodiment. Authentic casting would have reframed Porter’s interactions, with customers, employers, and his mother, as grounded in real disabled labor and emotional nuance, not symbolic perseverance. The film won awards but also became a case study in missed representation, especially given its focus on overcoming adversity.
Name: William H. Macy

Description: John Hurt was cast in the 1980 film The Elephant Man. John Merrick (historically Joseph Merrick) had severe physical differences due to a condition believed to be Proteus syndrome. His body was visibly asymmetrical, with extensive growths affecting his face, spine, and limbs. Merrick is the emotional centre of the film, which explores his mistreatment, isolation, and eventual dignity. His disability is not just physical, it’s socially constructed through the reactions of others. Hurt was not disabled and wore extensive prosthetics. While his performance was praised, the film became a landmark example of cripping-up. Authentic casting would have reframed Merrick’s relationship, especially with Dr. Treves and the hospital staff. The emotional arc of dignity and humanity would have carried deeper resonance if performed by someone with lived experience of disfigurement or disability. The film’s legacy is complicated: it raised awareness but reinforced the idea that disabled roles are best performed by disabled actors.
Name: John Hurt

Description: Ian McKellen has been cast in disabled as disabled characters twice.Ian McKellen as Walter in Walter (1982). Walter is portrayed as a man with a learning disability, living in institutional care. His cognitive impairment affects his speech, decision-making, and social interactions. Walter is a passive figure whose life is shaped by the systems around him. The film critiques institutionalisation and neglect, positioning Walter as a symbol of vulnerability. McKellen is not cognitively disabled. His portrayal relies on physical and vocal mimicry, which critics have since described as patronising and reductive. Authentic casting would reframe Walter’s interactions with carers, family, and the institution as emotionally credible, allowing audiences to engage with disabled autonomy and systemic injustice. The film was praised at the time but is now viewed as emblematic of outdated representation practices.Ian McKellen as Richard III in Richard III (1995). Richard III is portrayed with a physical disability, traditionally a hunchback and limp. Shakespeare’s text amplifies this, linking deformity with villainy and ambition for political effect. Richard is the central figure, a manipulative and charismatic monarch whose disability is used to justify his moral corruption, but this is not without reason as he had grown up experiencing ableism and ridicule. McKellen is not physically disabled. His performance is powerful, but the production missed the opportunity to interrogate the play’s ableism through authentic embodiment. Casting a disabled actor would have reframed Richard’s power dynamics as rooted in lived experience, challenging the audience to separate disability from villainy. The role remains one of the most contested in disability representation, with calls for disabled-led reinterpretations. Even though Richard is a historical figure the play exaggerates his condition and is the first ever text to explore ableism. This way the literal diagnosis of Richard's condition is irrelevant and the role can be transposed to any physical condition.
Name: Ian McKellen
Known For: The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring

Description: Al Pacino was cast as Lt. Col. Frank Slade in Scent of a woman (1992). Slade is blind due to a military accident. His blindness is permanent and affects his mobility, independence, and emotional state. Slade is a bitter, charismatic veteran who forms a bond with a young student. His arc explores redemption, mentorship, and emotional vulnerability. Pacino is not blind or vision impaired. His portrayal won an Oscar but drew criticism for stylised blindness, especially in scenes of movement and emotional intensity. Authentic casting would have reshaped Slade’s mentorship and emotional breakdowns as grounded in disabled masculinity, not theatrical bravado. The film’s legacy is mixed: celebrated for performance, but in terms of contemporary practice the portrayal has become very dated.
Name: Al Pacino

Description: Julian Bleach was cast as Davros in Dr Who 2008 to 2015. Davros is a disabled scientist whose body is severely impaired. He has one functioning hand, a cybernetic eye, and relies on a mobile life-support chair. His lower body is absent, and he cannot survive outside the chair. Davros is a recurring antagonist, creator of the Daleks, and a symbol of twisted genius. His disability is central to his visual identity and narrative menace. Bleach is not disabled, continuing a tradition of non-disabled actors portraying Davros. While the character is iconic, his disability is stylised as monstrous and threatening. Authentic casting would have reframed Davros’s intellect and ideology, not as a product of impairment, but as a complex disabled identity. Despite his status as a disability icon, the show has never cast a disabled actor in the role, drawing criticism from UK disability advocates.
Name: Julian Bleach

Description: LeVar Burton cast as Geordi La Forge in Star Trek: The Next Generation (1987 to 1994), Star Trek: Picard (2023), Star Trek: Generations (1994), Star Trek: First Contact (1996), Star Trek: Insurrection (1998) and Star Trek: Nemesis (2002). Geordi is blind due to a congenital condition. He uses a VISOR (Visual Instrument and Sensory Organ Replacement) to perceive electromagnetic signals, effectively bypassing his optic nerves. Geordi is Chief Engineer of the Enterprise, a brilliant, empathetic leader whose blindness is normalised within the futuristic setting. His disability is not a barrier to competence or authority. Burton is not blind or vision impaired. While Geordi’s character was groundbreaking for its time, the casting still reflects a non-disabled lens. Burton himself noted that other actors related to him differently once the VISOR was removed. Authentic casting would have reframed Geordi’s relationships, especially with Data and Barclay, allowing audiences to engage with disabled leadership as lived experience. The role is often cited as progressive, but disability advocates have called for deeper embodiment and authentic casting in future iterations for Geordie and other disabled characters in the Star Trek universe.
Name: LeVar Burton

Description: Kevin McHale was cast as Artie Abrams in Glee (2009 to 2015). Artie is a wheelchair user due to a spinal cord injury sustained in childhood. His disability is permanent and affects his mobility and social dynamics. Artie is a core member of the glee club; intelligent, witty, and musically talented. His disability is occasionally explored through storylines about access, dating, and dreams. McHale is not a wheelchair user ur is physically disabled. The casting drew criticism for sidelining disabled performers and for musical numbers that showed Artie walking in fantasy sequences. Authentic casting would have reshaped Artie’s relationships with Tina, Brittany, and the ensemble, allowing audiences to engage with disabled youth culture as truth, not stylised metaphor. The show’s progressive tone was undercut by its reliance on cripping-up, despite occasional attempts at disability awareness.
Name: Kevin McHale

Description: Adam Scott was cast as Robbie in My Blind Brother (2016). Robbie is blind due to an unspecified condition. He is portrayed as confident, athletic, and emotionally complex. Robbie is a competitive athlete and the object of romantic tension between his brother and a woman they both pursue. His blindness is central to the film’s emotional and comedic dynamics. Scott is not blind or vision impaired. While the film avoids pity, it still relies on non-disabled mimicry for its emotional beats. Authentic casting would have reframed Robbie’s relationships as grounded in disabled embodiment, allowing audiences to witness real-world navigation, intimacy, emotions ,politics and rivalry. The film received mixed reviews, with some critics noting the missed opportunity for authentic representation.
Name: Adam Scott

Description: Helena Bonham Carter was cast as Jane Hatchard in The Theory of Flight (1998). Jane has motor neurone disease (MND), a progressive neurological condition that affects movement, speech, and eventually breathing. Her disability is degenerative and affects every aspect of her autonomy. Jane is a woman seeking sexual experience before her condition worsens. Her relationship with a failed artist explores desire, mortality, and emotional intimacy. Bonham Carter is not physically disabled. Her portrayal was stylised, and the film was criticised for fetishising disability and framing it through a non-disabled lens. Authentic casting would have reshaped Jane’s emotional arc, especially her vulnerability, agency, and intimacy as grounded in lived experience, not performance. The film’s premise sparked debate about disability and sexuality and why disabled actors are rarely cast as romantic leads or sexual partners in drama and movies. Unfortunately the casting choices undermined the movie's credibility and emotional truth.
Name: Helena Bonham Carter
Known For: Sweeney Todd: The Demon Barber of Fleet Street

Description: Vanessa Redgrave was cast as Blanche Hudson in the 1991 remake of Whatever Happened to Baby Jane?  Blanche is a wheelchair user due to a spinal injury sustained in a car crash. Her disability is permanent and affects her mobility and independence. Blanche is the emotionally restrained sister, trapped in her home and psychologically tormented by Jane. Her disability is central to the power dynamics and emotional tension of the story. At the time Redgrave did not have a physical disability. Authentic casting would have reframed Blanche’s relationship with Jane, not just as psychological warfare, but as a confrontation between embodied vulnerability and emotional cruelty, allowing audiences to engage with disabled sisterhood as lived experience.
Name: Vanessa Redgrave

Description: Bryce Dallas Howard was cast as Ivy Walker in The Village (2004). Ivy is blind due to a congenital condition. She navigates her world through sound, touch, and intuition. Her blindness is permanent and central to her emotional and narrative function. Ivy is the film’s protagonist. A brave, intuitive woman who ventures beyond her community to save a loved one. Her blindness is portrayed as mystical and symbolic of purity and courage. Howard is not vision impaired. Authentic casting would have reshaped Ivy’s journey, not as stylised bravery, but as a grounded act of disabled agency, allowing audiences to witness her emotional resilience as truth. The film was commercially successful, but disability advocates noted the missed opportunity for authentic representation.
Name: Bryce Dallas Howard

Description: Gary Oldman cast as Rolfe in Tip Toes (2003). Rolfe has dwarfism, a genetic condition affecting bone growth and stature. His disability is permanent and affects his physicality and social experience. Rolfe is the brother of the protagonist and a central figure in the film’s exploration of family, identity, and acceptance. His disability is central to the plot and emotional tension. Oldman is not disabled and performed the role on his knees with prosthetics. This casting drew widespread condemnation for its insensitivity and erasure, especially given that Peter Dinklage, who has dwarfism, was also in the cast. Authentic casting would have reframed Rolfe’s relationships with his brother, girlfriend, and community, as grounded in disabled embodiment, not mimicry. The film was critically panned and remains one of the most cited examples of offensive casting in disability cinema.Oldman was also cast as Mason Verger in Hannibal (2001). Verger is a quadriplegic with severe facial disfigurement, resulting from a violent attack. He uses a ventilator and is physically dependent on others for care. Verger is the film’s antagonist. A wealthy, vengeful man seeking to capture and torture Hannibal Lecter. His disability is grotesque and it is his vulnerability, a result of his own perversions and relationship with Lecter. Oldman is not physically disabled. Authentic casting would have allowed audiences to engage with disabled villainy as complex. The film was commercially successful, but disability representation and casting of Verger was criticised.
Name: Gary Oldman

Description: Michael Reid MacKay was cast as Jason 143 in X-Men 2 (2003). Jason is a motor-disabled mutant who uses a wheelchair and has limited physical movement. His condition is the result of experimentation and psychic manipulation, and he is non-verbal, communicating through illusion. Jason is weaponised by William Stryker to manipulate Professor Xavier. His psychic abilities are central to the film’s climax, but his body is treated as passive and instrumental. MacKay is not a wheelchair user or physically disabled. Authentic casting would have reframed Jason’s relationship with Xavier not as a plot device, but as a moment of mutual recognition between two minds navigating power and vulnerability. If cast authentically his presence could have challenged the franchise’s tendency to stylise disability as threat or tragedy without the depth of lived experience.
Name: Michael Reid MacKay

Description: Anna Paquin was cast as Rogue in X-Men (2000) and X-Men 2 (2003).  Rogue cannot touch others without absorbing their life force and memories. Her condition is metaphorical but deeply resonant with disability identity themes of isolation, bodily autonomy, and social exclusion. Rogue is a young mutant struggling with her identity and power. Her arc explores fear, intimacy, and self-acceptance, often serving as the emotional anchor for the ensemble. Paquin is not disabled, and Rogue’s condition is treated as a metaphor for adolescence and difference rather than recognising it's parallels with the lives of people with disability, especially people with conditions that impact immune systems, where human contact comes with risk. While powerful, this framing risks appropriating disability experience without embodiment. Authentic casting could have reframed Rogue’s relationships with Logan, Bobby, and Jean as emotionally grounded in lived experience of touch deprivation and social stigma. Her arc mirrors real-world disability narratives, but lacks the nuance of disabled authorship. The character remains iconic, but disability advocates have called for more explicit acknowledgment of her metaphorical resonance.Paquin also played Ada McGrath in The Piano (1993). Ada is mute, communicating through sign language and piano playing. Her muteness and afasia is congenital or trauma-induced (the film is ambiguous), and she expresses herself through non-verbal channels. Ada is the film’s protagonist, a woman navigating love, autonomy, and artistic expression in colonial New Zealand. Her disability is central to her emotional and narrative power. Paquin is not disabled and was not fluent in sign language prior to filming. Authentic casting would reshape Ada’s relationships with Flora, Baines, and Stewart as grounded in disabled communication and agency, allowing audiences to engage with non-verbal intimacy and lived truth. The film won multiple awards, but disability representation was largely framed through aesthetics rather than embodiment, and by more contemporary standards of representation it lacks truth.
Name: Anna Paquin

Description: James Marsden was cast as Scott Summers AKA Cyclops in the X-Men series; X-Men (2000), X2: X-Men United (2003), X-Men: The Last Stand (2006) and X-Men: Days of Future Past (2014). Cyclops has a vision impairment that causes uncontrollable optic blasts. He uses a specialised visor to regulate his power, an assistive technology that enables autonomy and safety. Scott is a team leader and romantic rival, often portrayed as emotionally restrained and tactically precise. His disability is stylised as power, but rarely explored emotionally. Marsden is not disabled. The role treats Cyclops’s impairment as superpower, sidelining the emotional and relational impact of assistive dependence. Authentic casting would have reframed Scott’s leadership and intimacy not as stoic control, but as lived negotiation between embodiment and responsibility, especially in scenes with Jean and Logan. The franchise’s visual emphasis on tech over emotion missed a chance to explore disabled relational depth.
Name: James Marsden

Description: Belén Rueda was cast as Julia Levin in Julia's Eyes (2010). Julia experiences progressive vision loss due to a degenerative condition. Her impairment affects depth perception, mobility, and emotional stability, especially under stress. Julia is the protagonist of a psychological thriller. Her disability heightens suspense, vulnerability, and isolation as she investigates her sister’s death while losing her sight. Rueda is not blind or vision impaired. The film uses visual techniques (blurring, darkness, framing) to simulate her experience, but her performance relies on mimicry. Authentic casting would have reframed Julia’s relationships with her husband, doctors, and the antagonist as grounded in real-world experience allowing audiences to witness disabled embodiment as truth.
Name: Belén Rueda

Description: Denzel Washington was cast as Eli in The Book of Eli (2010). Eli is blind or low-vision, navigating a post-apocalyptic world through heightened auditory and spatial awareness. His blindness is revealed gradually and used as a narrative twist. Eli is a lone wanderer protecting a sacred book. His disability is central to the film’s themes of faith, perception, and resilience though the lens of mysticism. Washington is not vision impaired. Authentic casting would have reframed Eli’s journey, not as stylised heroism, but as a grounded portrayal of blindness, adaptation, and moral clarity, especially in scenes of spiritual reflection.Denzel Washington was cast as Lincoln Rhyme in The Bone Collector (1999). Rhyme is a quadriplegic forensic expert, paralysed from the neck down after a spinal injury. He uses assistive technology (including a sip-and-puff interface) to communicate and work. Rhyme is the intellectual lead in a serial killer investigation. His disability is central to the film’s tension, balancing vulnerability, control, and mental acuity. Washington is not physically disabled. While the film avoids overt pity, it stylises Rhyme’s condition as a dramatic constraint. Authentic casting would have reshaped Rhyme’s mentorship of Amelia and his emotional arc not as a performance or limitation, but as a lived negotiation of power, intimacy, and mortality, especially in scenes of medical crisis and investigative brilliance.
Name: Denzel Washington

Description: Ron Perlman as Salvatore in Name of the Rose (1986). Salvatore is physically disabled, with impaired mobility and speech. His embodiment is marked by visible difference and social marginalisation within the monastic hierarchy and society in general. Salvatore is a supporting character whose disability amplifies his outsider status. He is treated with suspicion and ultimately persecuted, reinforcing themes of fear and exclusion. Perlman is not physically disabled. Authentic casting would have reframed Salvatore’s interactions as grounded in a lived understanding of marginalisation, allowing audiences to engage with disabled persecution as historical reality.
Name: Ron Perlman

Description: W. Earl Brown as Warren in There’s Something About Mary (1998). Warren is portrayed as autistic and intellectually disabled. He has sensory sensitivities (notably around his ears) and limited verbal communication. Warren is Mary’s brother and a source of emotional grounding. His presence shapes the romantic dynamics and adds unexpected depth. Brown is not disabled. While Warren is treated with affection, authentic casting would have reframed Warren’s relationships, not as quirky plot devices, but as emotionally credible bonds, especially with Mary and Ted. His sensory responses and protective instincts could have been portrayed with greater nuance if the role had been cast authentically with a neurodivergent actor.
Name: W. Earl Brown

Description: Andy Serkis was cast as Ian Dury in Sex & Drugs & Rock & Roll (2010).  Ian Dury had polio, resulting in lifelong physical impairment. He used a leg brace and walked with difficulty. His disability shaped his identity, activism and humour. Dury is the protagonist, a punk icon whose disability informs his music, relationships, and political voice. The film explores his childhood in institutional care and his adult defiance. Serkis is not disabled. While his performance was widely praised, sensitive and brilliant, some disability advocates questioned the casting choice. Authentic casting would have grounded Dury’s embodiment, not just in movement, but in the emotional labor of visibility, stigma, and resistance, especially in scenes of intimacy and public defiance. The film’s success shows it is possible for non-disabled actors to deliver powerful portrayals and really get under the skin of disability, but it also highlights the need for disabled-led biopics to shift industry norms. Serkis's performance is outstanding, like Day Lewis in My Left Foot, however this also highlights that performances like this are exceptions rather than the rule.
Name: Andy Serkis
Known For: War for the Planet of the Apes

Description: Rupert Everett was cast as Patrick in My Policeman (2022).  Patrick is a stroke survivor and wheelchair user. His speech is limited, and he requires assistance with daily tasks. Patrick is the older version of a central character in a love triangle. His disability is used to evoke sympathy and reflect on past injustices, especially around queer persecution. Everett is not disabled. Authentic casting would have reshaped Patrick’s relationships with Tom and Marion, as grounded in disabled aging, emotional memory, and embodied resilience, allowing audiences to engage with queer disability as lived history.
Name: Rupert Everett

Description: Gina McKee Played Bella, a wheelchair user in Notting Hill (1999).  Bella is a wheelchair user due to an unspecified condition. Her disability is permanent and affects her mobility and social interactions. Bella is a close friend of the protagonist, offering emotional support and comic timing. Her disability is treated with quiet dignity, not as a source of pity. McKee is not disabled. While her performance was praised for subtlety, the role remains one of the few disabled women in rom-coms. Authentic casting would have reframed Bella’s friendships and romantic history, challenging the genre’s tendency to exclude disabled desire and agency. The film's casting missed the chance to model inclusive casting in mainstream romance.
Name: Gina McKee

Description: Raymond Burr was cast as Robert T. Ironside in Ironside (1967 to 1975) and The Return of Ironside (1993). Ironside is a paraplegic police detective who uses a wheelchair. His disability is physical and acquired, central to his identity as a crime solver. Ironside’s disability is framed as a challenge he overcomes through intellect and grit. The show positions him as a stoic, cerebral figure whose wheelchair becomes symbolic of resilience rather than a lived reality. Raymond Burr was neither a wheelchair user nor was he physically disabled, and his portrayal lacked the nuance of lived experience. The show’s success in the 1960s was groundbreaking in visibility, but it also reinforced the idea that disability could be “performed” by non-disabled actors. Authentic casting could have deepened the audience's relationship with the character by showing the emotional and physical realities of navigating crime scenes, authority, and vulnerability. The 2013 reboot faced backlash again for casting Blair Underwood, also non-disabled, with producers citing flashback logistics as justification, however these could have been achieved with an ambulant wheelchair user, body doubling and imaginative direction.
Name: Raymond Burr

Description: Dominique Pinon was cast as Vriess in Alien: Resurrection (1997). Vriess is a spaceship mechanic who uses a wheelchair. His disability is physical, and he adapts his environment with ingenuity, including weaponised mobility technology. Vriess is portrayed as resourceful and sardonic, often using humour and mechanical skill to assert his value. His disability is not central to the plot but adds texture to the ensemble. Pinon, a non-disabled actor, played Vriess with stylized flair, but the performance lacked the grounded realism of someone with lived experience. Authentic casting could have reframed Vriess’s interactions especially his camaraderie and defiance as more than quirky resilience. It would allow the audience to see disability not as a costume but as a perspective, enriching the group dynamics aboard the ship. There is however a pivotal moment when the crew member with whom his gets the most ableist schtick from, turns out to be a friend who would lay down his life to save him. Unlike many other disabled characters in other movies Vriess is a person first who happens to enter the room on wheels.
Name: Dominique Pinon

Description: Sean Penn was cast as Sam Dawson in I am Sam (2001). Sam has an intellectual disability, likely developmental, affecting his cognitive processing and social interactions. The portrayal is overt and central to the story. Sam is a father fighting for custody of his daughter. His disability is the emotional and legal fulcrum of the film, used to explore themes of love, competence, and societal bias. Penn’s performance was widely criticised for being overly mannered and emotionally manipulative. Director Jessie Nelson later admitted she would not cast a non-disabled actor today. Authentic casting could have transformed the film’s emotional arc especially the father-daughter bond, into something more grounded and less performative. It would challenge audiences to confront their biases through genuine connection.
Name: Sean Penn

Description: Kalki Koechlin was cast as Laila in Margarita with a Straw (2014).  Laila has cerebral palsy, a neurological condition caused by trauma at birth, affecting motor function and speech. The film explores her physical challenges alongside her emotional and sexual awakening. Laila is a complex protagonist navigating disability, bisexuality, and cultural identity. Her journey is intimate, raw, and intersectional. Koechlin’s performance was praised for its sensitivity, but she is not physically disabled or have cerebral palsy. Director Shonali Bose required months of physical immersion, yet critics and disability advocates noted the missed opportunity for authentic casting. A disabled actor could have brought deeper nuance to Laila’s relationships especially her romantic and familial ones, by embodying the tension between independence and vulnerability with lived truth. From the audiences' perspective authentic casting would have been less performative and more grounded in truth, challenging their own assumptions and biases as well as those of the other characters.
Name: Kalki Koechlin

Description: Elizabeth Hartman was cast Selina D'Arcey in A Patch of Blue (1965). Selina is blind due to an accident in childhood. Her condition is permanent and affects her mobility, independence, and social interactions. Selina is a young woman living in poverty and abuse. Her blindness is central to the film’s emotional arc, especially her relationship with Gordon (Sidney Poitier), which explores race, care, and liberation. Hartman was not blind or vision impaired. Authentic casting would have reframed Selina’s relationships as lived negotiation of trust, autonomy, and emotional growth, especially in scenes of tactile intimacy and escape. While the film was praised for its progressive racial themes, disability representation was largely unexplored.
Name: Elizabeth Hartman

Description: Daniel Day-Lewis was cast as Christy Brown in My Left Foot (1989). Christy Brown had cerebral palsy, with limited control over his body except for his left foot. His condition was lifelong and shaped every aspect of his communication, mobility, and artistic practice. Christy is the protagonist of this biopic, which traces his journey from isolation to literary and artistic acclaim. His disability is central to the film’s themes of resilience, creativity, and familial tension. Day-Lewis was not disabled. While his performance is widely considered one of the most physically accurate portrayals of disability on screen, the casting remains a point of contention. Director Jim Sheridan has since acknowledged that he would cast differently today. Authentic casting would have reshaped Christy’s embodiment as lived experience of fatigue, frustration, and triumph, especially in scenes of artistic creation and love. The film was critically acclaimed, but its legacy is now part of broader debates about representation ethics.
Name: Daniel Day-Lewis

Description: Salma Hayek was cast as Frida Kahlo in Frida (2002).  Frida Kahlo lived with chronic pain and mobility impairments due to spina bifida, polio and a traumatic bus accident. She used braces, corsets, and a wheelchair, and her disability was central to her art and activism. Frida is portrayed as a passionate, politically engaged artist whose disability informs her aesthetic and emotional life. Her physical condition is depicted but not deeply embodied. Hayek is neurodivergent but not physically disabled. Casting her in the role of a visibly disabled icon is a case of cross-disability miscasting. Authentic casting would have reframed Frida’s relationship with Diego Rivera, her lovers, and her political peers. It would also connected on a deeper level with the audience through lived defiance.
Name: Salma Hayek

Description: Kenneth Branagh was cast as Dr. Arliss Loveless Wild Wild West (1999). Loveless is a wheelchair user with mobility impairments following a war injury. His condition is permanent and stylised through steampunk prosthetics and mechanical augmentation. Loveless is the film’s antagonist, a brilliant, vengeful scientist whose disability is exaggerated for theatrical menace. His embodiment is used as a visual and narrative device. Branagh is not a wheelchair user or disabled. Authentic casting would have reshaped Loveless’s power not as grotesque spectacle, but as disabled accomplishment and strategic brilliance, challenging the audience to see disability without a barrier, similar in concept to Davros in Doctor Who.
Name: Kenneth Branagh

Description: Woody Harrelson was cast as Larry Flynt in the movie The People vs. Larry Flynt (1996). Larry Flynt became a wheelchair user after surviving an assassination attempt in 1978, which left him with permanent spinal damage and chronic pain. His mobility was severely restricted, and he often used a gold-plated wheelchair. Flynt is portrayed as a provocative publisher and free speech advocate. His disability is central to the film’s second half, shaping his legal battles, public persona, and emotional volatility. Harrelson is not physically disabled. Authentic casting would have reframed Flynt’s relationshipswith Althea, his legal team, and the audience, as a lived embodiment of his negotiation of pain, and political agency, especially in scenes of courtroom confrontation and personal breakdown. Director Miloš Forman’s stylized approach emphasised Flynt’s eccentricity over his disabled lived experience.
Name: Woody Harrelson

Description: Hallie Eisenberg was cast as Helen Keller in The Miracle Worker (2000). Helen Keller was deafblind from infancy, with no sight or hearing. Her sensory impairments shaped her communication, education, and activism. Helen is the central figure in a biographical drama about her early life and breakthrough with teacher Anne Sullivan. Her disability is portrayed as both challenge and catalyst. Eisenberg is not disabled. The role relies on performed sensory impairment, continuing a tradition of casting non-disabled actors in Keller’s role. Authentic casting would have reframed Helen’s interactions as a disabled child navigating embodiment, frustration, and learning, allowing audiences to engage with sensory difference as lived truth.
Name: Hallie Eisenberg

Description: Renée Zellweger was cast as Jane in My Own Love Song (2010). Jane is a former singer who uses a wheelchair due to a spinal injury. Her mobility impairment is permanent and affects her independence and emotional resilience. Jane embarks on a road trip with her friend Joey, confronting trauma and rediscovering her voice. Her disability is central to the film’s themes of healing, love and self-expression. Zellweger is not a wheelchair user. The role uses disability as emotional weight, with Jane’s condition symbolising loss and recovery. Authentic casting would have reshaped Jane’s journey as a disabled woman reclaiming agency and creative identity. The film received mixed reviews, and disability advocates noted the missed opportunity for inclusive casting.
Name: Renée Zellweger

Description: Sophie Marceau was cast as Muriel in Cartagena (2009). Muriel is a tetraplegic woman, bed-bound due to a spinal injury. She has profound motor and mobility disabilities, requiring full-time care and assistive support. Muriel is a reclusive former boxer’s employer who teaches him to read and gradually reclaims emotional agency. Her disability is central to the film’s emotional arc and themes of interdependence. Marceau is not physically disabled. While her performance was praised for emotional nuance, the role relies on performed immobility. Authentic casting would have reshaped Muriel’s relationship with Léo, as a disabled woman navigating care, intimacy, love and autonomy, especially in scenes of emotional vulnerability.
Name: Sophie Marceau

Description: Nick Stahl was cast as Isaac Knott in Quid Pro Quo (2008). Isaac is a semi-paralyzed radio reporter who uses a wheelchair. His disability is the result of a childhood accident and is central to his identity and emotional journey. Isaac investigates a subculture of “wannabe” disabled people, leading to a surreal exploration of embodiment, fetishism, and self-perception. Stahl is not physically disabled. Although the film producers said that there was an inclusive casting process, the final choice missed the opportunity to cast an ambulant wheelchair user. Authentic casting would have reframed Isaac’s investigation, not as performance, but as lived inquiry into identity, embodiment, and community, especially in scenes of intimacy and psychological tension. The film received mixed reviews, and disability advocates noted the missed opportunity despite the film’s thematic ambition.
Name: Nick Stahl

Description: Daniel Newman was cast as Elias Riddler in Riddler’s Moon (1998). Elias is a wheelchair user with a mobility impairment. His condition is permanent and central to his identity and relationship with his mother. Elias is the son of a single mother living on a failing farm. His disability is part of the family’s hardship, but he also plays a key role in the film’s emotional and supernatural themes. Newman is not physically disabled. The role uses disability as emotional weight, with Elias’s condition symbolising vulnerability and resilience. Authentic casting would have reshaped Elias’s relationship with his mother, not as a burden, but as a disabled child navigating agency, care, and identity, especially in scenes of supernatural transformation.
Name: Daniel Newman

Description: Fiona Dourif was cast as the main protagonist Nica Pierce in The Curse of Chucky (2013), The Cult of Chucky (2017) and Chucky the TV series (2021 to 2024).  Nica is a paraplegic wheelchair user, born with her condition. Her mobility is restricted, and she navigates both physical and psychological trauma throughout the franchise. Nica is the protagonist and eventual antagonist, surviving Chucky’s attacks and later becoming possessed. Her disability is central to her vulnerability and transformation. Dourif is not disabled. Authentic casting would have reshaped Nica’s survival and possession as disabled agency and resistance, especially in scenes of escape, confrontation, and psychological breakdown. The franchise has been praised for queer and gender representation, but disability casting remains a gap.
Name: Fiona Dourif

Description: Thundercat was cast as The Modifier in The Book of Boba Fett (2021). The Modifier is implied to have a physical disability, operating in a subculture where body parts are replaced or enhanced with cybernetics. His own embodiment is partially augmented, suggesting lived experience with prosthetic adaptation. He is a technician and body mod artist, responsible for saving Fennec Shand’s life through cybernetic reconstruction. He represents the gateway to survival and transformation in the series’ techno-organic landscape. Thundercat is not physically disabled. While his casting brought cultural cachet, the role leans into disability as cool aesthetic, rather than embodied reality. Authentic casting would have reframed The Modifier’s interactions, not just as a stylist, but as a disabled artisan navigating ethics, embodiment, and care, especially in scenes of reconstruction and consent.
Name: Thundercat

Description: Timothy Olyphant was cast as Cobb Vanth in The Book of Boba Fett (2021-2022). While not a Mod himself, Vanth is associated with the group and is critically injured, requiring cybernetic intervention. His survival depends on assistive technology, aligning him with themes of bodily reconstruction. Vanth is a marshal and ally to Boba Fett. His injury and recovery arc position him as a bridge between able-bodied leadership and the Mod subculture. Olyphant is not disabled. His injury is used as a plot device, reinforcing disability as temporary setback. Authentic casting would have reshaped Vanth’s recovery, not as heroic return, but as a disabled man navigating identity, leadership, and embodiment.
Name: Timothy Olyphant

Description: Tim Pocock was cast as Cyclops in X-Men Origins: Wolverine (2009). Cyclops has a vision impairment that causes uncontrollable optic blasts. He must wear a specialised visor or ruby-quartz glasses to prevent involuntary destruction. His condition is permanent and requires constant assistive technology. In this prequel, a young Scott is abducted for experimentation. His power is portrayed as dangerous and uncontrollable, positioning him as a victim and asset. Pocock is not disabled. The role treats Cyclops’s impairment as a superpower, not a lived experience of assistive dependence. Authentic casting would have reframed Scott’s early trauma, not just as spectacle, but as a metaphor for disabled adolescence, where autonomy and bodily control are contested. His interactions with Logan and Emma Frost could have been more emotionally grounded through lived experience and fear.
Name: Tim Pocock

Description: Sophie Thatcher was cast as Drash in The Book of Boba Fett (2022). Drash is a Mod with visible cybernetic enhancements, replacing missing body parts. Her disability is permanent and stylized through chrome and circuitry. Drash is the leader of the Mods, a streetwise, loyal fighter who joins Boba Fett’s cause. Her embodiment is central to her identity and visual presence. Thatcher is not physically disabled. The role uses disability as fashion and cybernetic cool. Authentic casting would have reframed Drash’s leadership not as aesthetic rebellion, but as disabled agency, struggle and community-building.
Name: Sophie Thatcher

Description: Jordan Bolger was cast as Skad in The Book of Boba Fett (2022). Skad is a Mod with a cybernetic eye and other enhancements. His disability is permanent and stylised, functioning as both assistive tech and identity marker. Skad is a loyal member of the Mods, participating in combat and tactical support. His embodiment is part of the group’s visual and thematic cohesion. Bolger is not disabled. The role continues the pattern of disability as augmentation, sidelining lived experience and identity. Authentic casting would have reshaped Skad’s camaraderie as deeper solidarity and rebellion against attitudes.
Name: Jordan Bolger

Description: Jamie Bell was cast as Smike in Nicholas Nickleby (2002). Smike is portrayed with cognitive and physical impairments, likely neurodivergence and mobility limitations. He is emotionally vulnerable, socially isolated, and physically frail. Smike’s condition is compounded by chronic neglect and abuse at Wackford Squeers’s school, where he is beaten, underfed, and denied education; this institutional cruelty deepens his physical frailty and passivity and explains much of his distrust and learned helplessness, but even so he becomes Nicholas’s loyal companion. His suffering and death are central to the novel’s emotional arc. Bell is not disabled. Authentic casting would have reframed Smike’s loyalty and vulnerability especially in scenes of friendship and defiance. Physical abuse still happens a lot to vulnerable disabled people and this is a character that connects with disabled audiences and is important to disabled literary history.
Name: Jamie Bell

Description: Mare Winningham was cast as Helen Keller in Helen Keller: The Miracle Continues (1984). Helen Keller was deafblind from infancy due to illness. She communicated through tactile sign language and became a prolific author, lecturer, and disability rights activist. The film focuses on Keller’s adult life, including her education, activism, and emotional relationships. Her sensory impairments are central to her identity and public legacy. Winningham is neither deaf nor blind nor disabled. Authentic casting would have reshaped Keller’s interactions. While the film was praised for expanding Keller’s story beyond childhood, disability representation was not critically examined, and the casting choice reflects broader industry norms of exclusion.
Name: Mare Winningham

Description: Robert Cecil, 1st Earl of Salisbury in Gunpowder (2017). Cecil had a pronounced spinal curvature and mobility impairment, likely due to scoliosis or kyphosis. Historical accounts describe him as physically frail but intellectually formidable. Queen Elizabeth I's nicknames for Robert Cecil were my pygmy and my elf. These nicknames were due to his short stature and hunchback, a result of scoliosis. Cecil is the chief minister and spymaster under King James I, orchestrating surveillance and suppression of the Gunpowder Plot. His disability is visually referenced but not explored in depth. Mark Gatiss, a non-disabled actor, portrayed Cecil. The role minimises his physical condition, reinforcing disability as historical footnote rather than an identity. Authentic casting would have reframed Cecil’s political manoeuvring, not just as intellect, but as embodied resilience navigating courtly power structures, allowing audiences to engage with his lived experience and the ableism he would have experienced. While Gatiss’s performance was praised, the opportunity to explore disability as part of Cecil’s political identity was missed.
Name: Mark Gatiss

Description: John Leguizamo cast as Toulouse-Lautrec in Moulin Rouge! (2001). Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec had a genetic disorder (likely pycnodysostosis) that caused brittle bones and stunted growth. He was 4'11 and lived with chronic pain and mobility limitations. Toulouse-Lautrec is a bohemian artist and emotional anchor in the film’s ensemble. His disability is referenced visually by the actor being on his knees to simulate the artist's stature. Leguizamo is not physically disabled and wore prosthetics to appear shorter. While his performance was praised, the casting relied on physical mimicry rather than embodiment. Authentic casting would have reshaped Toulouse-Lautrec’s relationships as grounded in disabled artistry and social marginalisation, allowing audiences to engage with his legacy as both creative and political.
Name: John Leguizamo

Description: Andrew Tiernan as Ephialtes in 300 (2006) and 300: Rise of an Empire (2014). Ephialtes is physically disabled, with spinal and limb deformities that affect his posture and movement. He is portrayed as unable to lift a shield in the Spartan phalanx formation. Ephialtes is a tragic figure who seeks acceptance among the Spartans but is rejected due to his body. His arc turns from loyalty to betrayal, driven by ableist exclusion and humiliation. Tiernan is not physically disabled. Authentic casting would have reiforced Ephialtes’s rejection as a lived experience of systemic ableism, allowing audiences to engage with his emotional arc as grounded in truth. The film faced criticism from disability scholars for its portrayal of Ephialtes, however an authentic approach to casting would have reframed and grounded the performance.
Name: Andrew Tiernan

Description: Christopher Lee was cast as the Tiresias in The Odyssey in 1997.  In Greek mythology Tiresias was a prophet of Apollo in Thebes. Tiresias is blind, a prophet whose lack of sight is linked to spiritual insight. His blindness is permanent and central to his mythological identity. Tiresias guides Odysseus through prophecy and wisdom. Lee was not blind or vision impaired. Authentic casting would have reshaped Tiresias’s authority, not as mystical exception, but as lived wisdom, challenging the audience to see blindness as knowledge, not metaphor.
Name: Christopher Lee
Known For: Star Wars: Episode II - Attack of the Clones

Description: Damaris Lewis was cast as Komand’r / Blackfire in Titans (2019–2021). Blackfire cannot metabolize solar radiation, preventing her from flying, a core ability of her species. This congenital limitation leads to social exclusion and political disenfranchisement. Blackfire is a complex antagonist whose resentment of Starfire stems from systemic ableism. Her arc explores power, identity, and familial trauma. Lewis is not disabled. The role uses alien disability as metaphor, echoing real-world exclusion. Authentic casting would have reframed Blackfire’s bitterness and ambition, not as villainy, but as a disabled woman navigating systemic rejection, especially in scenes of confrontation and reconciliation. The show touched on these themes but did not foreground disability representation.
Name: Damaris Lewis

Description: Lee Thompson Young was cast as Victor Stone / Cyborg Smallville (2006–2010). Victor is injured in a car accident and rebuilt with cybernetic implants. His body is enhanced but visibly altered, requiring adaptation and secrecy. Victor appears in a few episodes as a reluctant hero grappling with identity and control. His disability is stylised as power, but his emotional arc is underdeveloped. Young was not disabled. The role uses cybernetics as origin story, sidelining the emotional complexity of prosthetic embodiment. Authentic casting would have reshaped Victor’s interactions, allowing audiences to engage with bodily difference as more than tech spectacle.
Name: Lee Thompson Young

Description: Joivan Wade was cast as Victor Stone / Cyborg Doom Patrol (2019–2023). Victor has extensive cybernetic prosthetics following a traumatic injury. His body is partially mechanical, requiring constant adaptation and emotional negotiation of identity. Victor is a core member of the Doom Patrol, navigating trauma, agency, and belonging. His arc includes a pivotal decision to remove his enhancements and reclaim a more human appearance. Wade is not disabled, but Doom Patrol was praised for its nuanced disability representation, but it missed the opportunity to authentically cast. Victor’s journey explores prosthetic embodiment, grief, and autonomy. Authentic casting would have deepened Victor’s relationships with Silas, Rita, and the team and resonated with disabled fans. I could have been grounded in lived experience, dependence on assistive technology and bodily negotiation, especially in scenes of vulnerability and transformation. Wade’s performance was widely respected, but the show’s broader disability themes highlight the missed opportunity for disabled-led casting.
Name: Joivan Wade

Description: Esai Morales was cast as Slade Wilson / Deathstroke, Titans (2019). Slade is canonically blind in one eye and has sustained multiple physical injuries. His body is augmented but visibly impaired, often portrayed with a limp or prosthetic support. Slade is a complex antagonist. Strategic, emotionally volatile, and driven by family trauma. His physical impairments are  part of his combat identity and moral ambiguity. Morales is not physically disabled. The show minimises Slade’s impairments, focusing on his tactical prowess and emotional manipulation. Authentic casting would have reshaped Slade’s relationship with his children, not just as a failed father, but as a man navigating trauma and embodiment, allowing for richer emotional nuance. The casting was celebrated for diversity, but disability representation was largely overlooked.
Name: Esai Morales
Known For: Mission: Impossible - Dead Reckoning Part One

Description: Sir Clifford Chatterley in Lady Chatterley's Lover (2015). Clifford is paraplegic due to a war injury. He uses a wheelchair and requires assistance with mobility and daily care. His disability is permanent and affects his physical independence and sexual function, although the latter could be psychological. Clifford is Lady Chatterley’s husband, intellectual, emotionally distant, and increasingly isolated. His disability is central to the novel’s exploration of class, intimacy, and bodily autonomy. In the 2015 BBC adaptation, Clifford was portrayed by James Norton, a non-disabled actor. The role leans into disability as emotional and it focuses on Clifford's self-image and self-worth. Authentic casting would have reframed Clifford’s relationship with Connie as a complex negotiation of intimacy, embodiment, and emotional distance, allowing audiences to engage with disabled desire and vulnerability as lived truth.
Name: James Norton

Description: John Malkovich was cast as Lennie Small in Of Mice and Men (1992). Lennie has an intellectual disability. Lennie exhibits traits consistent with an intellectual disability. He has limited cognitive processing, struggles with impulse control, and depends heavily on George for guidance and protection. His disability is central to the plot. It shapes his vulnerability, his relationship with George, and ultimately leads to the tragic ending. Lennie’s portrayal has been widely discussed in disability studies.
Name: John Malkovich

Description: Charlie Cox was cast as Matt Murdock / Daredevil in Daredevil (Netflix, 2015–2018). Matt is blind due to a childhood accident. He uses echolocation-like senses to navigate the world, which grant him superhuman perception. Medically, he is blind; socially, his enhanced senses negate many access barriers, although he keeps these hidden. He masks his condition, which is something many disabled people will relate to as they mask their to try to avoid prejudice and ableism. Matt is a lawyer by day and vigilante by night. His blindness is central to his identity, but the show emphasises his competence, moral conflict, and duality. Cox is not vision impaired. While his performance was widely praised, the casting drew criticism from blind and low-vision communities for excluding disabled actors from a rare leading role. Authentic casting would have reframed Matt’s relationships as grounded in real-world embodiment. It would have challenged assumptions about blindness and competence, especially in courtroom and combat scenes, however there is an argument that unlike other disabled characters such as Dr Mid-Nite, Matt does not use assistive technologies but has an additional sense that is equivalent to sight, and he uses his blindness to hide this. This makes the character more complex in terms of disability culture and identity.
Name: Charlie Cox

Description: Ray Walston was cast as Candy in Of Mice and Men (1992). Candy is an aging ranch worker who lost one hand in a farm accident. His disability symbolises obsolescence and economic vulnerability. He fears being discarded and clings to the dream of owning land with George and Lennie. Candy’s portrayal reflects 1930s attitudes toward disabled labourers, who were seen as expendable and pitied. A disabled actor could have grounded the role authentically.
Name: Ray Walston

Description: Joe Morton was cast as Crooks in Candy in Of Mice and Men (1992). He is described as having a crooked spine, which is the origin of his nickname. Steinbeck refers to him as a cripple in the text, and his back injury limits his mobility and physical labor capacity. This disability, combined with his status as the only Black character on the ranch, places Crooks at the intersection of racial and ableist marginalisation. His isolation and exclusion are central to his portrayal, and his physical impairment is used narratively to reinforce his social vulnerability.
Name: Joe Morton

Description: Dustin Hoffman as Raymond Babbitt in Rain Man (1988). Raymond is an autistic savant with limited verbal communication, rigid routines, and exceptional memory. His disability and neurodivergence is central to the plot and emotional arc. Raymond is the catalyst for his brother Charlie’s transformation. His traits drive the narrative tension, but his perspective is sidelined in favour of Charlie’s redemption. Hoffman is not neurodivergent. His performance won an Oscar but drew criticism for codifying autism through mimicry. Authentic casting would have reframed Raymond’s relationships, not as a puzzle to be solved, but as a person to be understood, allowing audiences to engage with autistic embodiment as truth. The film sparked widespread awareness but also entrenched stereotypes about savantism and emotional detachment, whereas many autistic people are deeply empathetic but struggle with communicating emotions.
Name: Dustin Hoffman

Description: Eddie Izzard was cast as Silver in Treasure Island (2012). Silver is an amputee, traditionally portrayed with a missing leg and use of a crutch. His disability is permanent and part of his pirate identity. Silver is charismatic, cunning, and morally ambiguous. His impairment is part of his visual iconography and tactical persona. Izzard does not have a physical disability. Authentic casting would have reshaped Silver’s leadership and manipulation not as theatrical bravado, but as lived resilience, allowing audiences to engage with disabled cunning and charisma.
Name: Eddie Izzard

Description: Keith Allen was cast as Pew in Treasure Island (2012). Pew is blind, navigating the world through sound and touch. His blindness is permanent and portrayed as part of his menace and mystery. He is a feared pirate who delivers the Black Spot, a symbol of death. His blindness is used to heighten tension and unpredictability. Allen is not blind or vision impaired. Authentic casting would have reframed Pew’s menace as embodied power, challenging the audience to see blind agency beyond fear.
Name: Keith Allen

Description: Jacob Elordi was cast as the creature in Frankenstein (2025). The Creature is physically disfigured and cognitively fragmented, assembled from dead bodies and rejected by society. His disability is both literal (bodily difference, pain, speech difficulty) and symbolic (social exclusion, lack of identity, otherness, ableism). He is the emotional and philosophical core of the story, seeking connection, recognition, and dignity. His suffering is intensified by his creator’s refusal to name or accept him. Elordi is not physically disabled. Authentic casting would have reframed the Creature’s relationship with Victor, not as monstrous rejection, but as a confrontation with ableist creation and abandonment. Audiences would engage with the Creature’s emotional depth as lived experience, not stylised despair. Early commentary raised concerns about erasure and missed opportunity, especially given the story’s legacy as a metaphor for disability and otherness.
Name: Jacob Elordi

Description: Daniel Radcliffe was cast as Igor in Victor Frankenstein (2015). In earlier adaptations, Igor is a character portrayed with a hunched back and mobility impairment, often coded as disabled, loyal and subservient. In this version, Radcliffe’s Igor begins with a spinal deformity that is surgically corrected early in the film. Igor is reimagined as a brilliant assistant and emotional anchor for Victor.
