His disability is treated through a non-disabled lens as a temporary obstacle, erased to enable his narrative function, whereas his narrative function could have happened regardless of his disability, if anything having a disability would have made the character and his achievements more interesting. Radcliffe is neurodivergent but is not physically disabled, and the film removes Igor’s impairment entirely. This is a clear case of disability erasure. Authentic casting with an actor with a physical disability and retention of Igor’s disability, would have reshaped his bond with Victor as one of mutual dependence and embodied difference. The film’s attempt to modernise the character missed a chance to interrogate ableism in science and storytelling or have a more modern perspective of disability identity.
Name: Daniel Radcliffe
Known For: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows: Part 2

Description: Spencer Wilding cast as The Creature in Victor Frankenstein (2015). The Creature is constructed from multiple human bodies and is physically deformed. He experiences chronic pain, cognitive dissonance, and profound social rejection. His disability is both physical and existential. He is the embodiment of Victor’s ambition and guilt, a being who seeks recognition, companionship, and identity. His suffering and rejection drive the emotional and philosophical core of the narrative. Wilding is not physically disabled. The role is heavily stylised, with prosthetics and CGI used to create the Creature’s appearance. Authentic casting would have reframed the Creature’s isolation, not as a metaphor for monstrosity, but as a lived experience of being visibly different, rejected for how he looks and socially excluded. His relationship with Victor could have been a powerful exploration of creator and creation, or parent and child, through the lens of ableism and bodily autonomy. The film was criticised for flattening the novel’s emotional complexity, and the Creature’s portrayal was seen as more spectacle than substance.
Name: Spencer Wilding

Description: Shane Briant cast as Sir Clifford Chatterley in Lady Chatterley's Lover (1981). Clifford is paraplegic due to a war injury. He uses a wheelchair and is sexually and emotionally distant, relying on intellectual pursuits and social status to act as his mask. Clifford’s disability is central to the novel’s exploration of intimacy, class, and bodily autonomy. His emotional detachment and physical limitations drive Connie’s affair with Mellors. Briant is not physically disabled. Authentic casting would have reshaped Clifford’s relationship with Connie not as symbolic impotence, but as a complex negotiation of intimacy, embodiment, and emotional distance, allowing audiences to engage with disabled desire and vulnerability.
Name: Shane Briant

Description: Eric Stoltz was cast as Joel Garcia in The Waterdance (1992). Joel becomes tetraplegic after a hiking accident. He has limited mobility in his arms and no movement below the chest. His disability is permanent and central to his emotional and physical journey. Joel is the film’s protagonist, a writer navigating grief, identity, and adaptation in a rehabilitation center. His arc explores denial, intimacy, and the search for meaning post-injury. Stoltz is not disabled. While the film is semi-autobiographical (based on co-writer Neal Jimenez’s own experience), the casting choice reflects a missed opportunity for authentic embodiment. Casting a disabled actor would have reshaped Joel’s relationships, allowing audiences to engage with disabled masculinity and vulnerability as lived truth. The film was praised for its realism, but disability advocates have since questioned why lived experience wasn’t extended to casting.
Name: Eric Stoltz

Description: Wesley Snipes  cast as Raymond Hill in The Waterdance (1992). Raymond is paraplegic due to a spinal cord injury. He uses a wheelchair and is adjusting to life with paralysis, including changes in sexuality, independence, and identity. Raymond is charismatic, flirtatious, and emotionally guarded. His arc explores pride, denial, and the tension between self-image and reality. He serves as both foil and confidant to Joel. Snipes is not physically disabled. His performance is compelling, but the role relies on stylised physicality and emotional projection. Authentic casting would have reframed Raymond’s bravado and intimacy not as performance, but as lived complexity, especially in scenes of sexual frustration and emotional vulnerability. The film’s strength lies in its ensemble, but the absence of disabled actors limits its representational depth.
Name: Wesley Snipes

Description: William Forsythe was cast as Bloss in The Waterdance (1992). Bloss is paraplegic, with full upper-body mobility but no movement below the waist. His disability is permanent and affects his physicality and emotional regulation. Bloss is volatile, confrontational, and deeply wounded. He masks vulnerability with aggression, challenging both staff and fellow patients. His arc explores trauma, masculinity, and emotional repression. Forsythe is not disabled. His portrayal is intense but stylised, leaning into emotional extremes. Authentic casting would have reframed Bloss’s rage and tenderness not as theatrical contrast, but as embodied tension, allowing audiences to witness disabled anger and grief as truth. The character’s emotional complexity could have been even more resonant with lived experience behind the performance.
Name: William Forsythe

Description: Demetrius Grosse cast as Eric Williams / Grim Reaper in Wonder Man (2025). In the comics, Grim Reaper loses limbs and relies on cybernetic enhancements, including a scythe-like prosthetic arm. His disability is central to his transformation and combat identity. Eric is a complex antagonist, driven by grief, rivalry, and power. His limb loss is part of his origin and visual identity. Grosse is not physically disabled. Authentic casting would have reshaped Eric’s emotional arc, especially his bond with Wonder Man and his descent into vengeance, as grounded in disabled masculinity. Commentary from disability advocates has raised concerns about erasure and missed opportunity.
Name: Demetrius A. Grosse

Description: Elle Fanning was cast as Thia in Predator: Badlands (2025). Thia is an android whose body is split, her torso and legs operate independently due to damage. While not human, her disjointed embodiment mirrors limb loss and prosthetic reliance. Thia becomes a companion to Dek, a young Predator. Her fragmented body is used for slapstick combat and emotional bonding, including scenes where her limbs reunite to fight and celebrate. Fanning is not physically disabled. While the role is metaphorical, it visually evokes limb difference and mobility impairment. Authentic casting would have reframed Thia’s relationship with Dek, not just as quirky companionship, but as a mutual recognition of altered embodiment, allowing audiences to engage with disability-coded androids as more than comic relief. Reviews praised the emotional undercurrent but noted the stylisation of her physicality
Name: Elle Fanning

Description: Djimon Hounsou was cast as Caliban in The Tempest (2010). Caliban is often interpreted as physically and cognitively disabled, his body described as twisted, his speech as erratic. Shakespeare’s text frames him as subhuman and oppressed. Caliban is a servant and antagonist, representing colonial resistance and embodied otherness. His disability is metaphorical, but not casting authentically sidelines disability.
Name: Djimon Hounsou

Description: Kristen Wiig cast as Barbara Minerva, AKA Cheetah in Wonder Woman 1984 (2020). In the comics, Barbara Minerva suffers from chronic pain and mobility issues in her human form. She uses a cane and experiences physical limitations that contrast sharply with her superpowered Cheetah transformation. Barbara begins as a socially awkward academic who idolizes Diana. Her transformation into Cheetah is driven by a desire for strength, confidence, and freedom from pain. Her physical disability is erased in the film adaptation, replaced with social insecurity. Wiig does not have a physical disability, and the film omits Barbara’s mobility impairment entirely. This is a clear case of disability erasure. Authentic casting and retention of Barbara’s disability would have reframed her relationship with Diana as a complex interplay of embodiment, envy, and recognition, allowing audiences to engage with disabled desire and agency. The omission flattened Barbara’s emotional arc.
Name: Kristen Wiig

Description: Kris Kristofferson cast as Abraham Whistler in Blade (1998), Blade II (2002) and Blade: Trinity (2004). Whistler walks with a pronounced limp and uses a cane, attributed to nerve and bone damage. His disability is permanent and visibly affects his mobility. Whistler is Blade’s mentor and weapons expert, a grizzled, world-weary figure who provides emotional grounding and tactical support. His disability is part of his rugged persona but is rarely explored beyond surface-level physicality. Kristofferson was not physically disabled. The limp is performed rather than embodied, and the cane becomes a visual shorthand for age and toughness rather than a lived experience of disability. Authentic casting would have reframed Whistler’s relationship with Blade, not just as mentor and protégé, but as two men navigating physical trauma and resilience in different ways. It would have added emotional realism to scenes of pain, endurance, and sacrifice.
Name: Kris Kristofferson

Description: Warren Mitchell cast as Barquentine in Gormenghast (2000). Barquentine is a physically disabled character who uses a crutch and has a twisted body, often described as grotesque in the source material. His disability is congenital and affects his mobility and posture. He is the Master of Ritual in the castle of Gormenghast, an eccentric, authoritarian figure who upholds ancient traditions. His disability is used to emphasise his otherness and severity. Mitchell was not disabled. Authentic casting would have reframed Barquentine’s authority and isolation not as theatrical oddity, but as a reflection of lived marginalisation within a rigid system. His interactions with Steerpike and the castle hierarchy could have carried deeper emotional and political weight.
Name: Warren Mitchell

Description: Tye Sheridan was cast as Scott Summers AKA Cyclops in X-Men: Apocalypse (2016) and Dark Phoenix (2019). As in earlier portrayals, Scott’s optic blasts require assistive technology to manage. His condition isolates him emotionally and physically, especially in romantic relationships. Scott is a central team member and love interest to Jean Grey. His arc explores leadership, loyalty, and emotional restraint, with his disability stylised as a burden and a weapon. Sheridan is not disabled. The films continue to frame Cyclops’s condition as power with a cost, rather than a disability requiring adaptation. Authentic casting would have reshaped Scott’s relationships with Jean, Charles, and the team as grounded in mutual negotiation of access, trust, and control, allowing audiences to engage with disability as layered and embodied.
Name: Tye Sheridan

Description: Arnold Schwarzenegger was cast as Mr. Freeze AKA Dr. Victor Fries, in Batman and Robin (1997). Victor Fries is dependent on a cryogenic life-support suit due to a lab accident. He cannot survive at normal temperatures and relies on assistive technology for mobility and survival. Fries is a tragic villain driven by love for his terminally ill wife, Nora. His disability is framed as both his curse and his motivation, and portrayed through icy aesthetics and gadgetry. Schwarzenegger is not physically disabled. The role uses disability as visual metaphor, a cold exterior masking emotional depth. Authentic casting would have reframed Fries’s grief, isolation, and technological dependence as grounded in real-world disabled embodiment, allowing audiences to engage with his emotional arc as lived truth.
Name: Arnold Schwarzenegger

Description: Kerry Washington was cast as Alicia Masters in Fantastic Four (2005). Alicia is blind, relying on touch and sound to sculpt and navigate. Her blindness is permanent and central to her emotional and artistic identity. She is Ben Grimm’s love interest, offering emotional support and acceptance. Her blindness is used to highlight her ability to “see” Ben’s humanity beyond his appearance. Washington is not vision impaired. Authentic casting would have reshaped Alicia’s relationship with Ben, not as symbolic acceptance, but as mutual recognition of embodied difference, allowing audiences to witness disabled intimacy and agency.
Name: Kerry Washington

Description: Thomas Kretschmann cast as Baron Von Strucker in Avengers: Age of Ultron (2015). In the comics, Strucker has a cybernetic arm and other implants due to injury and augmentation. Strucker is a HYDRA leader and early antagonist. His physical modifications are part of his persona and identity. Kretschmann is not physically disabled, and the film omits Strucker’s impairments entirely. This is a case of disability erasure. Authentic casting and retention of Strucker’s cybernetic embodiment would have reframed his power and ideology as shaped also by trauma and adaptation.
Name: Thomas Kretschmann

Description: James Badge Dale was cast as Eric Savin / Coldblood in Iron Man 3 (2013). Savin is a U.S. Army colonel who loses limbs in a landmine explosion and is rebuilt with cybernetic implants. His condition is permanent and existentially traumatic. Savin is a henchman for Aldrich Killian. His resentment of his disability is used to justify aggression, self-loathing and is the reason for his emotional detachment. Dale is not physically disabled. The role ignores the emotional complexity of limb loss and adaptation. Authentic casting would have reshaped Savin’s arc as a confrontation with bodily autonomy, grief, and identity, allowing audiences to engage with disabled embodiment beyond spectacle.
Name: James Badge Dale

Description: Nick Zano was cast as Nate Heywood AKA Citizen Steel in Legends of Tomorrow (2016 to 2022) and Arrow (2016). In the comics, Nate Heywood loses a leg and gains a metallic prosthetic through trauma and mutation. His physical disability is central to his origin and powers. In the show, Nate is reimagined as fully able-bodied, erasing his disability entirely. His powers are presented as transformation, not adaptation. Zano is not physically disabled. The show’s version of Nate omits his amputation and prosthetic embodiment, a clear case of disability erasure. The omission drew criticism from fans familiar with the comics.
Name: Nick Zano

Description: B.J. Novak was cast as Alistair Smythe in The Amazing Spider-Man 2 (2014). In the comics, Smythe is paralysed from the waist down and later encases himself in a bioorganic carapace to regain mobility. His disability is permanent and technologically mitigated. Smythe is a scientist and antagonist, driven by ambition and resentment. His disability is part of his transformation into a supervillain. Novak is not physically disabled, and the film minimises Smythe’s impairment. Authentic casting would have reshaped Smythe’s arc, not as menace, but as a complex negotiation of power, access, and identity, allowing audiences to engage with disabled embodiment as multifaceted and traumatic.
Name: B.J. Novak

Description: Alicia Silverstone cast as Barbara Gordon in Batman & Robin (1997). In the comics, Barbara Gordon becomes paraplegic after being shot by the Joker, later taking on the mantle of Oracle, a wheelchair-using tech strategist. In Batman & Robin, however, Silverstone’s Barbara is reimagined as Alfred’s niece and remains able-bodied throughout. Barbara is portrayed as a rebellious teen who becomes Batgirl. Her disability arc is entirely omitted, erasing Oracle’s legacy as one of the most prominent disabled superheroes. Silverstone is not a wheelchair user or is physically disabled, and the film bypasses Barbara’s paraplegic identity. This is a clear case of disability erasure. Authentic casting and retention of Oracle’s narrative would have reframed Barbara’s relationships with Batman, Alfred, and Robin as grounded in disabled agency, technological mastery, and emotional resilience, challenging the genre’s tendency to equate heroism with physical prowess. Scholars have critiqued this omission as a missed opportunity for feminist and disability representation.
Name: Alicia Silverstone

Description: Régis Royer was cast as Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec in Lautrec (1998). Toulouse-Lautrec had a genetic disorder (likely pycnodysostosis) that caused brittle bones and stunted growth. He was 4'11, lived with chronic pain, and had visible physical differences. he film explores Lautrec’s artistic life and romantic relationships, particularly with Suzanne Valadon. His disability is central to his social marginalisation and emotional intensity. Royer is not disabled. The role uses prosthetics and camera angles to simulate Lautrec’s stature. Authentic casting would have reframed Lautrec’s relationship with Valadon, his family, and the Montmartre community as grounded in lived experience of physical difference and social exclusion, allowing audiences to engage with his creativity and vulnerability as embodied truth. While the film was praised for its visual style, it missed the opportunity to center disabled artistry through authentic performance
Name: Régis Royer

Description: Cynthia Nixon was cast as Emily Dickinson in A Quiet Passion (2016). Dickinson lived with epilepsy, chronic illness, and visible facial differences. These conditions contributed to her reclusive lifestyle and shaped her poetic voice. The film portrays Dickinson’s intellectual rigour, emotional intensity, and social isolation. Her health conditions are depicted as part of her inner life and poetic sensibility. Nixon is not disabled. While her performance was widely praised, the role stylises Dickinson’s illness as poetic suffering. Authentic casting would have reframed Dickinson’s solitude and creativity not as tragic eccentricity, but as a disabled woman’s negotiation of embodiment, gender, and artistic legacy, especially in scenes of physical decline and spiritual defiance.
Name: Cynthia Nixon

Description: Daniel Evans cast as Robert Cecil, 1st Earl of Salisbury in The Virgin Queen (2006). Robert Cecil, 1st Earl of Salisbury, had a pronounced spinal curvature, likely scoliosis or kyphosis, resulting in visible physical difference and mobility impairment. Historical accounts describe him as physically frail but politically formidable. Cecil is a key strategist and advisor to Queen Elizabeth I, navigating court politics and succession crises. His disability is visually referenced but not explored as part of his identity or leadership. Evans is not physically disabled. The portrayal minimises Cecil’s physical condition, reinforcing disability as historical footnote. Authentic casting would have reframed Cecil’s political manoeuvring, not just as intellect, but as embodied resilience navigating power structures, allowing audiences to engage with disabled leadership as lived experience and exploring ableist attitudes in a period context when there was no identity of being a disabled person as disabled as a word did not exist, instead visibly disabled people were referred to as crippled or monstrous.
Name: Daniel Evans

Description: James Wilby cast as Sir Clifford Chatterley in Lady Chatterley (1993) Sir Clifford is paraplegic due to a war injury. He uses a wheelchair and requires assistance with mobility and daily tasks. Clifford is Lady Chatterley’s husband. He is intellectual, emotionally distant, and sexually unavailable. His disability is central to the novel’s exploration of intimacy, class, and bodily autonomy. Wilby is not physically disabled. The role leans into the character's disability as emotional and sexual inadequacy. Authentic casting would have reshaped Clifford’s relationship with Connie, not as symbolic impotence, but as a complex negotiation of intimacy, embodiment, loss and emotional distance, allowing audiences to engage with disabled desire and vulnerability as lived truth.
Name: James Wilby

Description: Anthony Hopkins cast as Quasimodo in The Hunchback of Notre Dame (1982). Quasimodo has a severe spinal deformity and facial difference. His physical condition leads to social isolation and emotional trauma. Quasimodo is the emotional heart of the story. He is misunderstood, loyal, and yearns for connection. His disability is central to the narrative’s themes of beauty, justice, prejudice and compassion. Hopkins is not physically disabled. Authentic casting would have reframed Quasimodo’s relationships with Esmeralda, Frollo, and the public as grounded in disabled embodiment and social rejection, challenging audiences to see disabled humanity beyond pity or spectacle.
Name: Anthony Hopkins

Description: Ben Tibber was cast as Tiny Tim in A Christmas Carol (1999). Tiny Tim is a child with a mobility impairment, often depicted using a crutch and suffering from an unnamed chronic illness. His condition is terminal without intervention. Tim is the emotional heart of the story, his vulnerability and optimism catalyse Scrooge’s transformation. He represents innocence, suffering, and moral clarity. Tibber is not disabled. Authentic casting would have reframed Tim’s relationship with his family not as symbolic purity, but as a disabled child navigating care, joy, and community, allowing audiences to engage with his life beyond sentiment.
Name: Ben Tibber

Description: Karen Allen cast as Laura Wingfield in The Glass Menagerie (1987). Laura has a physical disability which causes her to limp, and she is emotionally fragile, often interpreted as neurodivergent. Her condition affects her confidence, mobility, and social engagement. Laura is the emotional center of the story, her fragility and longing shape the family’s dynamics and the tension with the gentleman caller. Her disability is symbolic of vulnerability and isolation. Allen is not physically disabled. Authentic casting would have reframed Laura’s interactions as a disabled woman navigating familial pressure and romantic hope, allowing audiences to engage with her agency and interiority.
Name: Karen Allen

Description: Heydon Prowse cast as Colin Craven in A Secret Garden (1993). Colin is a child with a psychosomatic illness, believed to be physically disabled and bedridden. His condition is portrayed as both emotional and physical, with eventual recovery. Colin is a central figure in the garden’s transformation, moving from isolation and fear to vitality and friendship. His disability is used to symbolise emotional repression and healing. Prowse is not physically disabled. The role leans into disability as temporary obstacle. Authentic casting would have reshaped Colin’s journey not as symbolic healing, but as a disabled child navigating care, agency, and friendship, allowing audiences to engage with disabled childhood as multifaceted.
Name: Heydon Prowse

Description: Rutger Hauer as Nick Parker in Blind Fury (1989). Nick is blind due to a war injury. He adapts through heightened senses and swordsmanship, modelled after the Japanese Zatoichi archetype. Nick is the protagonist, a wandering hero who protects a child and confronts injustice. Hauer was not vision impaired. Authentic casting would have reframed Nick’s navigation, combat, and emotional vulnerability going beyond a stylised spectacle, but as lived adaptation, especially in scenes of mentorship and conflict.
Name: Rutger Hauer

Description: Dina Meyer cast as Barbara Gordon in Birds of Prey (2002 to 2003). Barbara is paraplegic following an attack by the Joker. She uses a wheelchair and adaptive technology, operating as Oracle, a strategist and mentor. Barbara is the intellectual and emotional anchor of the team. Her disability is central to her transformation from Batgirl to Oracle, redefining heroism through tech, leadership, and resilience. Meyer is not physically disabled. While the show was praised for portraying Barbara as competent and powerful, it relied on performed embodiment. Authentic casting would have reshaped Barbara’s relationships with Helena, Dinah, and Alfred as a lived negotiation of access, trauma, and agency, especially in scenes of emotional vulnerability.
Name: Dina Meyer

Description: Craig Lamar Traylor as Stevie Kenarban in Malcolm in the Middle (2000 to 2006). Stevie is a wheelchair user with severe asthma. He speaks slowly and breathes through a medical device. His disability is permanent and affects mobility, speech, and social interaction. Stevie is Malcolm’s best friend. He is intelligent, witty, and emotionally grounded. His disability is treated with respect and humour, often challenging stereotypes. Traylor is not a wheelchair user or physically disabled. While the role avoids pity it relies on performed embodiment. Authentic casting would have deepened Stevie’s relationships with Malcolm, his parents, and teachers, especially in episodes about independence and overprotection.
Name: Craig Lamar Traylor

Description: Stanley Tucci as Captain Hook in Peter and Wendy (2015). Hook is canonically an amputee, having lost a hand to a crocodile. He wears a prosthetic hook, which is central to his identity and visual iconography. Hook is the antagonist, cunning, theatrical, and emotionally complex. His disability is stylised as wonderfully flamboyant menace and eccentricity. Tucci is not physically disabled. The role continues the tradition of disability as villainy, using limb difference as a visual shorthand for danger. Authentic casting would have reshaped Hook’s rivalry with Peter and his leadership of the pirates, not just as caricature, but as disabled agency and charisma, challenging the audience to see genuine limb difference without losing the captain's edge.
Name: Stanley Tucci

Description: Robert Carlyle as James I in Gunpowder, Treason & Plot (2004). James I had significant mobility impairments. Historical accounts describe delayed walking, erratic gait, and reliance on physical support. Possible causes include rickets or a hereditary neuromuscular disorder. James is portrayed as a politically astute monarch navigating religious conflict and succession. His physical condition is largely sidelined in favour of intellectual and strategic traits. Carlyle is not physically disabled. The portrayal minimises James’s physical impairments. Authentic casting would have reframed James’s relationships with courtiers, adversaries, and family as shaped by embodied vulnerability and political resilience, allowing audiences to engage with the idea of disability and royalty. This is disability erasure which happens regularly with portrayal of British kings including Charles I who had physical and mobility disabilities as well as had ‘macroglossia’, where his tongue was too large for his mouth affecting his ability to speak, eat and drink, and Henry VIII after his hunting accident age (44) when he ended up with permanent physical disabilities which resulted in him using a number of mobility aids such as dual walking sticks, an early type of wheelchair and a hoist and pulley system for getting upstairs.
Name: Robert Carlyle

Description: Cailee Spaeny as Simone Vivane in Wake Up Dead Man (2025). Simone is written as an ambulant wheelchair user, a character whose mobility fluctuates, who may stand or walk short distances, but for whom a wheelchair is a primary mobility aid. This type of disability is often misunderstood or flattened on screen, yet it offers rich narrative texture. It influences how other characters read her body, sometimes incorrectly.  Cailee Spaeny is not physically disabled. When disability is performed rather than lived, the relationships around the character are shaped by a non‑disabled lens. The other characters may respond to the performance of disability rather than the truth of it.The audience will sense the gap between portrayal and reality, which can limit the character's emotional depth. If the character has been authentically cast it would have influenced their relationships in ways that would have deepened emotional realism. For example, how others offer help, misjudge her capabilities, or learn to understand her boundaries can reveal their values and flaws.
Name: Cailee Spaeny

Description: David Jonsson as the android Andy in the film Alien: Romulus (2024). The character portrayed the character as initially having a damaged, malfunctioning persona that was widely interpreted as resembling a disability, including autism or a speech impediment.  Although Andy is not disabled in a contemporary and literal medical sense, android characters in the Alien universe consistently occupy a narrative and social position that parallels disability representation. They are designed bodies whose physicality is read as “other,” “less human,” or “functionally limited” by those around them. Their movement and sensory processing differ from human norms. They are subject to prejudice, mistrust, and objectification, often treated as tools rather than people. Their autonomy is constrained by programming, hierarchy, and expectation, a structural limitation that mirrors real‑world constraints placed on disabled people. Andy’s embodiment is a coded form of non‑normative existence, where the character’s physical and behavioural difference is central to how others perceive and interact with him. This makes the casting choice especially significant: the role requires an actor capable of conveying a body and mind that operate outside human norms without slipping into caricature or mechanical cliché. Andy’s embodiment is a coded form of non‑normative existence, where the character’s physical and behavioural difference is central to how others perceive and interact with him. This makes the casting choice especially significant: the role requires an actor capable of conveying a body and mind that operate outside human norms without slipping into caricature or mechanical cliché. Casting a disabled actor could have been a more interesting and appropriate creative choice.
Name: David Jonsson

Description: Nicholas Cassim as Bruce in Mr Inbetween (2018 to 2019). Bruce is written as living with an aggressive, progressive form of Motor Neurone Disease (MND). This type of MND affects Co‑ordination  – reduced fine motor control, difficulty initiating or sustaining movement, Mobility – increasing reliance on aids, altered gait, fatigue, and eventual loss of independent movement, Muscle strength and stability – changes in posture, balance, and the ability to perform everyday tasks, Speech and breath control (depending on progression) – shifts in vocal rhythm, clarity, and energy. Crucially, MND is not a static condition. It is dynamic, with physical changes occurring over time. This creates a specific embodied reality where the character's movements become slower, less predictable, and more effortful. Their body’s relationship with space changes. Everyday actions take on new rhythms and require adaptation. When portrayed authentically with an actor who has lived experience of motor control related disability such as brain injury or cerebral palsy, this condition becomes part of the character’s physical truth rather than a dramatic device.  Bruce’s home becomes a space where Ray’s emotional guard drops. The physical environment — chairs, mobility aids, the pace of movement — shapes the rhythm of their scenes. Bruce’s disability influences how Ray behaves. Ray listens more, and becomes protective without being patronising, shifting reveal Ray’s humanity and deepen the show’s emotional texture. Casting a non‑disabled actor to portray a character with progressive MND raises several interconnected concerns. A non‑disabled actor must simulate the physicality. Even with research and sensitivity, simulation risks: Over‑emphasising certain movements, missing the subtleties, creating a performance that feels externally constructed rather than internally lived. Authentic casting would bring a natural physical truth that cannot be replicated. It does not have to be the same condition, this is not a box ticking exercise, but an actor who lives with a motor related condition would have a deeper insight into the character's lived experience and how others would react to their changes and challenges, Authentic casting could have allowed: a richer, more textured portrayal of MND, a performance shaped by lived experience rather than external observation and a more complex emotional beats between Bruce and Ray This is not about “accuracy” alone — it is about expanding the emotional and creative palette of any show that portrays acquired and progressive conditions.
Name: Nicholas Cassim

Description: Christina Chang as Dr. Audrey Lim in The Good Doctor (2017–2024). Dr. Lim was stabbed twice in the Season 5 finale of The Good Doctor, an attack that caused damage to her spine. When Season 6 begins, it’s revealed that the injury left her paralysed from the waist down. Dr. Lim is shown using a wheelchair throughout the early part of Season 6 as she adapts to her new reality. Christina Chang is not a wheelchair user and for a role like this, if the character was known to eventually become a wheelchair user then casting an ambulant wheelchair user would have been a more inclusive choice. Many wheelchair users can walk for short distances and there are examples of productions where actors who are ambulant wheelchair users have been cast to at first play a non-disabled role that becomes a disabled role. As this was season 5 before the injury happened that it is unlikely that this story arc was planned in season 1, and therefore a non-disabled would be a reasonable and ethical choice. It is a very useful example of where casting a disabled actor in a non-disabled role that becomes disabled is a distinctive possibility.
Name: Christina Chang

Description: Freddie Highmore as Dr. Shaun Murphy in The Good Doctor. The show never treats his diagnosis of autism as a mystery or twist, it is part of the premise.  Freddie Highmore is not neurodivergent himself but the character is, and if the role was cast now not considering a neurodivergent actor for the role would be unlikely to contradict policy and commitments.
Name: Freddie Highmore

Description: Harvey Elder is a nuclear engineer and explorer who becomes the ruler of Subterranea after being rejected and ridiculed by the surface world. In the comics, he is short, very large-bodied and severely myopic, with extreme sensitivity to ordinary light; protective glasses and a radar-like sense allow him to navigate environments that would otherwise be inaccessible to him.Paul Walter Hauser played Mole Man in The Fantastic Four: First Steps (2025). The adaptation retained Harvey’s leadership of Subterranea and developed him into a misunderstood community leader and eventual ally, but it played down the visual impairment, photosensitivity, short stature and distinctive sensory experience that help define the comic-book character.A visually impaired actor or performer of short stature could bring practical knowledge to Harvey’s use of protective eyewear, his response to surface lighting and the contrast between moving confidently underground and encountering barriers above it. Casting someone with relevant lived experience would also help separate his disability from the older suggestion that bodily difference naturally produces rejection, resentment or villainy.Authentic casting could make Mole Man’s underground world feel like more than a refuge for an outcast: it could be understood as an environment in which his body and senses work differently, perhaps even better, than they do on the surface. That would deepen the creative contrast between how surface society sees Harvey and the capable leader, engineer and strategist he has become in a world designed around different assumptions.
Name: Paul Walter Hauser

Description: Destiny is the eldest of the Endless and the personification of everything that has happened, is happening and will happen within DC’s Sandman mythology. He appears as a blind, robed figure carrying the Book of Destiny—also known as the Cosmic Log—which is chained to his wrist and contains the complete course of existence; Destiny and the book are so closely connected that neither can meaningfully be understood without the other.Adrian Lester played Destiny in the second season of Netflix’s The Sandman in 2025. The series retained the character’s blindness, solemn physical presence and omniscient relationship with the book, but the casting is not publicly known to draw on blind lived experience.Destiny’s blindness is paradoxical because he possesses complete knowledge while lacking ordinary sight, creating a mythic form of disability rather than a direct representation of everyday visual impairment. This makes the casting creatively challenging, but it also creates an opportunity to distinguish between how a blind person physically moves through their immediate environment and how a cosmic being experiences all of time.A blind actor could have grounded Destiny’s orientation, stillness and physical relationship with the book while preserving the mystery of whether he cannot see or has moved beyond sight as humans understand it. Authentic casting would make his omniscience feel stranger and more powerful: the audience would recognise the truth of blindness in the performer’s body while understanding that Destiny’s knowledge comes from something far greater than vision.
Name: Adrian Lester

Description: In the second season of Titans, Rose Wilson (portrayed by Chelsea Zhang) is introduced as the daughter of the assassin Deathstroke. Unlike her DC comic book counterpart—who gouges out her own eye to prove her loyalty to her father—the television series alters her origin story. In Titans, Rose is recruited by Deathstroke to infiltrate the team as a mole. This operation comes at the cost of her left eye, leaving her with a permanent visual impairment that she conceals using an eyepatch both in her casual attire and her Ravager uniform. The show’s casting directors selected American actress Chelsea Zhang for the recurring role of Rose Wilson. Up to that point, Zhang was primarily known for her work as Brittany in the Disney Channel series Andi Mack, as well as her roles in independent films like Relish and Netflix’s Daybreak. Zhang is a sighted, non-disabled actress who does not have a visual impairment or monocular vision in her personal life. Casting a fully sighted actor to play a monocular character is considered a missed opportunity to provide employment to the severely underrepresented community of visually impaired performers.
Name: Chelsea Zhang

Description: In Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D he played Daniel Sousa, a war veteran and agent with the SSR (and later S.H.I.E.L.D.) who experiences prejudice due to his leg injury, he was created for Agent Carter (2015–2016). The actor does not have a physical disability or limb difference. In 1955, he first encounters the main time-travelling S.H.I.E.L.D. team after he encounters Jemma Simmons impersonating Peggy Carter, their relationship having ended. After preventing him from being assassinated by a Hydra agent sent by Wilfred Malick as he originally was in history, Sousa joins the team in their mission through time against the Chronicoms, entering a romantic relationship with Daisy Johnson after being trapped in a time loop. In the process, a new and more advanced prosthetic leg is built for him which enables him to walk and run normally again. One year after defeating the Chronicoms, Sousa joins the present day S.H.I.E.L.D. and continues to work alongside Daisy and Kora.
Name: Enver Gjokaj

Description: In the 2018 BBC adaptation, Philip Durrant, played by Matthew Goode, lost the use of his legs in a car crash. Although presented as a decorated former fighter pilot, his disability was not a war injury: he crashed while driving drunk after spending his wife Mary’s money at the races.In Agatha Christie’s original 1958 novel, Philip contracted polio, which paralysed his legs. The 2007 Agatha Christie’s Marple adaptation broadly retains this explanation.Dramatically, his acquired disability makes him financially and physically dependent on Mary and the Argyll family. This dependence contributes to his resentment, drinking and destructive behaviour, particularly in the 2018 version—although the adaptation problematically links his disability quite closely with bitterness and moral deterioration.
Name: Matthew Goode

Description: In John Wick:Chapter 4 he played Caine, a blind former assassin who once worked alongside John Wick. The High Table forces him to hunt John by threatening his daughter.Although Caine is highly skilled, he is not shown as a simple villain. He remains loyal to his daughter and has clear affection for John. His conflict comes from being forced to choose between friendship and his daughter’s safety.Caine uses sound, touch, memory and carefully placed objects to understand his surroundings. His blindness is central to the character and is clearly communicated to the audience.
Name: Donnie Yen
